Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 43, verses 1–8:

[Page 165]
(Surat al-Zukhruf)
It has eighty-nine verses and is Meccan.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Ha, Mim.﴾ ﴿By the Book that makes things clear.﴾ ﴿Indeed, We have made it an Arabic Qur'an, so that you may understand.﴾ ﴿And indeed it is, in the Mother of the Book with Us, exalted and full of wisdom.﴾ ﴿Shall We then turn away the Reminder from you, merely because you are a people who exceed the limits?﴾ ﴿And how many a prophet did We send among the earlier peoples.﴾ ﴿Yet no prophet came to them but they mocked him.﴾ ﴿So We destroyed those who were stronger in might than these, and the example of the earlier peoples has passed.﴾

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. ﴿Ha, Mim.﴾ ﴿By the Book that makes things clear.﴾ ﴿Indeed, We have made it an Arabic Qur'an, so that you may understand.﴾ ﴿And indeed it is, in the Mother of the Book with Us, exalted and full of wisdom.﴾ ﴿Shall We then turn away the Reminder from you, merely because you are a people who exceed the limits?﴾ ﴿And how many a prophet did We send among the earlier peoples.﴾ ﴿Yet no prophet came to them but they mocked him.﴾ ﴿So We destroyed those who were stronger in might than these, and the example of the earlier peoples has passed.﴾

Know that His saying ﴿Ha, Mim.﴾ ﴿By the Book that makes things clear.﴾ admits of two interpretations:

The first: the implied sense is "This is Ha, Mim. By the Book that makes things clear," so the oath falls upon the fact that this surah is the surah of "Ha, Mim," and His saying ﴿Indeed, We have made it an Arabic Qur'an﴾ begins a separate statement.

The second: the implied sense is: "This is Ha, Mim," then He said: ﴿By the Book that makes things clear. Indeed, We have made it an Arabic Qur'an﴾, so the thing sworn to is His saying ﴿Indeed, We have made it an Arabic Qur'an﴾.

Regarding the meaning of "the Book" there are two views. The first: it means the Qur'an, and on this reading He has sworn by the Qur'an that He made it Arabic.

The second: it means writing and script, and He swore by writing because of the great benefits in it, for the sciences were only perfected through script. When an earlier scholar derived a science and recorded it in a book, and a later scholar came and studied it, he could add to the derivation of benefits, and by this means the benefits multiplied and reached great ends. As for describing the Book as "clear" (mubin), there are several aspects:

The first: it is clear to those to whom it was sent down, because it is in their language and tongue.

The second: "clear" is that which makes clear the path of guidance from the path of error, and makes clear every chapter from what is other than it, and made it detailed and summarized.

[Page 166]
Know that describing it as "clear" is metaphorical, because the One who makes clear is Allah, Exalted, and the Qur'an was named thus in an extended sense, insofar as clarification has come about through it.

As for His saying ﴿Indeed, We have made it an Arabic Qur'an, so that you may understand﴾, there are several issues:

The first issue: those who hold that the Qur'an is created have argued from this verse in several ways:

The first: the verse indicates that the Qur'an is "made" (majʿul), and what is made is what is fashioned and created. If they say: why could it not be that what is meant is that He named it "Arabic"? We reply: this is refuted in two ways:

The first: if "making" meant this, it would follow that whoever named it "non-Arab" would become non-Arab even though it is in the language of the Arabs, and it is known that this is false.

The second: if "making" were turned to mean naming, it would follow that naming is made, and naming is also the speech of Allah, and that would imply that He made part of His speech; and if that holds of part, it holds of the whole.

The second: He described it as a Qur'an, and it was named a Qur'an only because He made some of it joined to other parts, and what is like that is fashioned and made.

The third: He described it as Arabic, and it is Arabic only because these words were specifically assigned to their referents by the convention and terminology of the Arabs, and that indicates that it is made and fashioned.

The fourth: swearing by other than Allah is not permissible, as is known, so the implied sense is: "Ha, Mim, and by the Lord of the Clear Book." This is reinforced by what is related, that he (peace be upon him) used to say: "O Lord of Ta-Ha and Ya-Sin, and O Lord of the Great Qur'an."

The answer: what you have mentioned is true, for you have only used these aspects to prove that these successive letters and consecutive words are originated and created, and that is known by necessity, and who disputes it with you? Rather, your argument amounts to proving what is already known to be established by necessity.

The second issue: the word "la'alla" (perhaps/so that) expresses hope and wish, and this is not fitting for one who knows the outcomes of affairs, so the intended meaning here is "in order that" (kay), i.e., We sent it down as an Arabic Qur'an so that you may understand its meaning and comprehend its import. The Mu'tazilah said: the sense of the statement becomes "Indeed, We sent it down as an Arabic Qur'an in order that you may comprehend its meaning," and this conveys two matters:

One: the acts of Allah Exalted are caused by purposes and motives.

The second: He, Exalted, sent down the Qur'an only that people may be guided by it, and this indicates that He, Exalted, intended guidance and knowledge from all, contrary to the view of those who say that He intended disbelief and turning away from some. Know that this type of Mu'tazilite argument is well known, and our answers to it are well known, so there is no benefit in repeating them, and Allah knows best.

The third issue: His saying ﴿so that you may understand﴾ indicates that the Qur'an is known and that there is nothing in it that is ambiguous and unknown, contrary to those who say: part of it is known and part of it is unknown.

* * *

Then Exalted Allah said: ﴿And indeed it is, in the Mother of the Book with Us, exalted and full of wisdom.﴾ There are issues here:

The first issue: Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "Immi al-Kitab" with a kasra on the alif, while the rest read it with a damma.

The second issue: the pronoun in His saying "wa-innahu" refers to the Book mentioned earlier in ﴿the Mother of the Book with Us﴾. Scholars differ regarding the meaning of "the Mother of the Book" in two views:

The first view: it is the Preserved Tablet, based on His saying ﴿Nay, it is a glorious Qur'an, in a Preserved Tablet﴾ [al-Buruj: 22].

[Page 167]
Know that on this interpretation, all the attributes mentioned here are attributes of the Preserved Tablet.

The first attribute: that it is the ﴿Mother of the Book﴾, and the reason is that the origin of everything is its mother. The Qur'an is recorded with Allah in the Preserved Tablet, then it was transcribed to the lowest heaven, then it was sent down in parts according to what was beneficial. From Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him: "The first thing Allah created was the pen, and He commanded it to write what He wished to create." So the Book is with Him. If it is said: what is the wisdom in creating this Preserved Tablet, given that He is the Knower of the unseen and forgetfulness and error are impossible for Him? We reply: when He recorded in it the rulings concerning the events of created things, and then the angels witness that all events happen in conformity with that written record, they infer from this the perfection of Allah's wisdom and knowledge.

The second attribute of the Preserved Tablet: His saying ﴿with Us﴾. Ibn 'Abbas mentioned it thus, and Allah specially honored it with this distinction because it is a book comprising the states of all things that come into being, as if it is the book that contains everything that occurs in the dominion and kingdom of Allah. Therefore it received this honor. Al-Wahidi said: it is possible that this is an attribute of the Qur'an, the meaning being: "Indeed it is, with Us, in the Mother of the Book."

The third attribute: that it is "exalted" (ʿaliyy), meaning elevated above the aspects of corruption and falsehood. It was also said: the meaning is that it is elevated above all books by reason of being a miracle that remains through time.

The fourth attribute: that it is "wise" (ḥakīm), meaning well-ordered in the aspects of eloquence and articulacy. It was also said: "ḥakīm" means possessing far-reaching wisdom. It was also said: all these attributes are attributes of the Qur'an, as we have mentioned.

The second view on the interpretation of "the Mother of the Book": it is the clear verses (muḥkamāt), based on the saying of Exalted Allah: ﴿It is He who has sent down to you the Book; in it are clear verses, they are the mother of the Book﴾ [Al 'Imran: 7]. The meaning is that the surah of "Ha, Mim" is situated among the clear verses, which are the origin and the mother.

* * *

Then Exalted Allah said: ﴿Shall We then turn away the Reminder from you, merely because you are a people who exceed the limits?﴾ There are issues here:

The first issue: Nafi', Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "in kuntum" with a kasra on the alif, its implied sense being: "If you are people who exceed the limits, We will not turn away the Reminder from you." It was also said: "in" here means "idh" (when), as in His saying: ﴿And leave what remains of usury, if you are believers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 278]. In sum: the condition is placed after the answer. The rest read it with a fatha on the alif, as a causal clause, meaning: "because you are people who exceed the limits."

The second issue: al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: one says "daraba 'anhu" and "adraba 'anhu," meaning "he left it" and "he withheld from it." His saying ﴿ṣafḥan﴾ means "turning away." The original sense is that you turn away with the side of your neck. On this basis, His saying ﴿Shall We then turn away the Reminder from you ṣafḥan﴾ has the implied sense: "Shall We then withhold Our withholding from you?" or the implied sense: "Shall We then pardon you with a pardon?" They differed concerning the meaning of "the Reminder": it was said it means "Shall We then withhold from you the remembrance of Allah's punishment?" It was said: "Shall We withhold from you the admonitions and exhortations?" It was said: "Shall We withhold from you the Qur'an?" This is an interrogative in the form of denial, meaning: "We will not leave off this warning, this admonition, because you are people who exceed the limits." Qatadah said: if this Qur'an had been lifted when the first of this community rejected it, they would have perished, but Allah in His mercy repeated it to them and called them to it for twenty years. Having understood this, we say: this statement admits of two interpretations:

The first: mercy, meaning We will not abandon you despite your bad choice, but We will remind you and admonish you until you return to the right path.

The second: an emphasis on severity, meaning: do you think you will be left alone with what you desire? No, rather We will hold you to action, call you to the religion, and take you to account whenever you neglect the obligation and commit the abomination.

The third issue: the author of "al-Kashshaf" said: the fa' in His saying ﴿Shall We then turn away﴾ is for coordination with an omitted element, its implied sense being: "Shall We let you be, and then turn away the Reminder from you?"

* * *

Then Exalted Allah said: ﴿And how many a prophet did We send among the earlier peoples.﴾ ﴿Yet no prophet came to them but they mocked him.﴾ The meaning is that the custom of nations with the prophets who call them to the true religion is denial and mockery. Therefore you should not be distressed by your people's insistence on denial and mockery, because when a calamity becomes general, it becomes lighter.

* * *

Then Exalted Allah said: ﴿So We destroyed those who were stronger in might than these﴾, meaning that those earlier peoples to whom Allah sent the messengers were stronger in might than the Quraysh, that is, greater in number and vigor. Then He said: ﴿and the example of the earlier peoples has passed.﴾ The meaning is that the disbelievers of Mecca followed in disbelief and denial the path of those before them, so let them beware lest there descend upon them the same disgrace that descended upon them. We have set forth their example for them, as He said: ﴿And to each We set forth parables﴾ [al-Furqan: 39], and as in His saying: ﴿And you dwelt in the dwellings of those who wronged themselves﴾ [Ibrahim: 45] up to His saying ﴿and We set forth for you the parables.﴾ And Allah knows best.

The second: it means writing and script, and He swore by writing because of the great benefits in it, for the sciences were only perfected through script. When an earlier scholar derived a science and recorded it in a book, and a later scholar came and studied it, he could add to the derivation of benefits, and by this means the benefits multiplied and reached great ends. The first: it is clear to those to whom it was sent down, because it is in their language and tongue.

The first: if "making" meant this, it would follow that whoever named it "non-Arab" would become non-Arab even though it is in the language of the Arabs, and it is known that this is false.

The second: if "making" were turned to mean naming, it would follow that naming is made, and naming is also the speech of Allah, and that would imply that He made part of His speech; and if that holds of part, it holds of the whole.

The second: He described it as a Qur'an, and it was named a Qur'an only because He made some of it joined to other parts, and what is like that is fashioned and made.

The third: He described it as Arabic, and it is Arabic only because these words were specifically assigned to their referents by the convention and terminology of the Arabs, and that indicates that it is made and fashioned.

The fourth: swearing by other than Allah is not permissible, as is known, so the implied sense is: "Ha, Mim, and by the Lord of the Clear Book." This is reinforced by what is related, that he (peace be upon him) used to say: "O Lord of Ta-Ha and Ya-Sin, and O Lord of the Great Qur'an."

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 43, verses 1–8:

[Page 165]
(Surat al-Zukhruf)
It has eighty-nine verses and is Meccan.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Ha, Mim.﴾ ﴿By the Book that makes things clear.﴾ ﴿Indeed, We have made it an Arabic Qur'an, so that you may understand.﴾ ﴿And indeed it is, in the Mother of the Book with Us, exalted and full of wisdom.﴾ ﴿Shall We then turn away the Reminder from you, merely because you are a people who exceed the limits?﴾ ﴿And how many a prophet did We send among the earlier peoples.﴾ ﴿Yet no prophet came to them but they mocked him.﴾ ﴿So We destroyed those who were stronger in might than these, and the example of the earlier peoples has passed.﴾

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. ﴿Ha, Mim.﴾ ﴿By the Book that makes things clear.﴾ ﴿Indeed, We have made it an Arabic Qur'an, so that you may understand.﴾ ﴿And indeed it is, in the Mother of the Book with Us, exalted and full of wisdom.﴾ ﴿Shall We then turn away the Reminder from you, merely because you are a people who exceed the limits?﴾ ﴿And how many a prophet did We send among the earlier peoples.﴾ ﴿Yet no prophet came to them but they mocked him.﴾ ﴿So We destroyed those who were stronger in might than these, and the example of the earlier peoples has passed.﴾

Know that His saying ﴿Ha, Mim.﴾ ﴿By the Book that makes things clear.﴾ admits of two interpretations:

The first: the implied sense is "This is Ha, Mim. By the Book that makes things clear," so the oath falls upon the fact that this surah is the surah of "Ha, Mim," and His saying ﴿Indeed, We have made it an Arabic Qur'an﴾ begins a separate statement.

The second: the implied sense is: "This is Ha, Mim," then He said: ﴿By the Book that makes things clear. Indeed, We have made it an Arabic Qur'an﴾, so the thing sworn to is His saying ﴿Indeed, We have made it an Arabic Qur'an﴾.

Regarding the meaning of "the Book" there are two views. The first: it means the Qur'an, and on this reading He has sworn by the Qur'an that He made it Arabic.

The second: it means writing and script, and He swore by writing because of the great benefits in it, for the sciences were only perfected through script. When an earlier scholar derived a science and recorded it in a book, and a later scholar came and studied it, he could add to the derivation of benefits, and by this means the benefits multiplied and reached great ends. As for describing the Book as "clear" (mubin), there are several aspects:

The first: it is clear to those to whom it was sent down, because it is in their language and tongue.

The second: "clear" is that which makes clear the path of guidance from the path of error, and makes clear every chapter from what is other than it, and made it detailed and summarized.

[Page 166]
Know that describing it as "clear" is metaphorical, because the One who makes clear is Allah, Exalted, and the Qur'an was named thus in an extended sense, insofar as clarification has come about through it.

As for His saying ﴿Indeed, We have made it an Arabic Qur'an, so that you may understand﴾, there are several issues:

The first issue: those who hold that the Qur'an is created have argued from this verse in several ways:

The first: the verse indicates that the Qur'an is "made" (majʿul), and what is made is what is fashioned and created. If they say: why could it not be that what is meant is that He named it "Arabic"? We reply: this is refuted in two ways:

The first: if "making" meant this, it would follow that whoever named it "non-Arab" would become non-Arab even though it is in the language of the Arabs, and it is known that this is false.

The second: if "making" were turned to mean naming, it would follow that naming is made, and naming is also the speech of Allah, and that would imply that He made part of His speech; and if that holds of part, it holds of the whole.

The second: He described it as a Qur'an, and it was named a Qur'an only because He made some of it joined to other parts, and what is like that is fashioned and made.

The third: He described it as Arabic, and it is Arabic only because these words were specifically assigned to their referents by the convention and terminology of the Arabs, and that indicates that it is made and fashioned.

The fourth: swearing by other than Allah is not permissible, as is known, so the implied sense is: "Ha, Mim, and by the Lord of the Clear Book." This is reinforced by what is related, that he (peace be upon him) used to say: "O Lord of Ta-Ha and Ya-Sin, and O Lord of the Great Qur'an."

The answer: what you have mentioned is true, for you have only used these aspects to prove that these successive letters and consecutive words are originated and created, and that is known by necessity, and who disputes it with you? Rather, your argument amounts to proving what is already known to be established by necessity.

The second issue: the word "la'alla" (perhaps/so that) expresses hope and wish, and this is not fitting for one who knows the outcomes of affairs, so the intended meaning here is "in order that" (kay), i.e., We sent it down as an Arabic Qur'an so that you may understand its meaning and comprehend its import. The Mu'tazilah said: the sense of the statement becomes "Indeed, We sent it down as an Arabic Qur'an in order that you may comprehend its meaning," and this conveys two matters:

One: the acts of Allah Exalted are caused by purposes and motives.

The second: He, Exalted, sent down the Qur'an only that people may be guided by it, and this indicates that He, Exalted, intended guidance and knowledge from all, contrary to the view of those who say that He intended disbelief and turning away from some. Know that this type of Mu'tazilite argument is well known, and our answers to it are well known, so there is no benefit in repeating them, and Allah knows best.

The third issue: His saying ﴿so that you may understand﴾ indicates that the Qur'an is known and that there is nothing in it that is ambiguous and unknown, contrary to those who say: part of it is known and part of it is unknown.

* * *

Then Exalted Allah said: ﴿And indeed it is, in the Mother of the Book with Us, exalted and full of wisdom.﴾ There are issues here:

The first issue: Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "Immi al-Kitab" with a kasra on the alif, while the rest read it with a damma.

The second issue: the pronoun in His saying "wa-innahu" refers to the Book mentioned earlier in ﴿the Mother of the Book with Us﴾. Scholars differ regarding the meaning of "the Mother of the Book" in two views:

The first view: it is the Preserved Tablet, based on His saying ﴿Nay, it is a glorious Qur'an, in a Preserved Tablet﴾ [al-Buruj: 22].

[Page 167]
Know that on this interpretation, all the attributes mentioned here are attributes of the Preserved Tablet.

The first attribute: that it is the ﴿Mother of the Book﴾, and the reason is that the origin of everything is its mother. The Qur'an is recorded with Allah in the Preserved Tablet, then it was transcribed to the lowest heaven, then it was sent down in parts according to what was beneficial. From Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him: "The first thing Allah created was the pen, and He commanded it to write what He wished to create." So the Book is with Him. If it is said: what is the wisdom in creating this Preserved Tablet, given that He is the Knower of the unseen and forgetfulness and error are impossible for Him? We reply: when He recorded in it the rulings concerning the events of created things, and then the angels witness that all events happen in conformity with that written record, they infer from this the perfection of Allah's wisdom and knowledge.

The second attribute of the Preserved Tablet: His saying ﴿with Us﴾. Ibn 'Abbas mentioned it thus, and Allah specially honored it with this distinction because it is a book comprising the states of all things that come into being, as if it is the book that contains everything that occurs in the dominion and kingdom of Allah. Therefore it received this honor. Al-Wahidi said: it is possible that this is an attribute of the Qur'an, the meaning being: "Indeed it is, with Us, in the Mother of the Book."

The third attribute: that it is "exalted" (ʿaliyy), meaning elevated above the aspects of corruption and falsehood. It was also said: the meaning is that it is elevated above all books by reason of being a miracle that remains through time.

The fourth attribute: that it is "wise" (ḥakīm), meaning well-ordered in the aspects of eloquence and articulacy. It was also said: "ḥakīm" means possessing far-reaching wisdom. It was also said: all these attributes are attributes of the Qur'an, as we have mentioned.

The second view on the interpretation of "the Mother of the Book": it is the clear verses (muḥkamāt), based on the saying of Exalted Allah: ﴿It is He who has sent down to you the Book; in it are clear verses, they are the mother of the Book﴾ [Al 'Imran: 7]. The meaning is that the surah of "Ha, Mim" is situated among the clear verses, which are the origin and the mother.

* * *

Then Exalted Allah said: ﴿Shall We then turn away the Reminder from you, merely because you are a people who exceed the limits?﴾ There are issues here:

The first issue: Nafi', Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "in kuntum" with a kasra on the alif, its implied sense being: "If you are people who exceed the limits, We will not turn away the Reminder from you." It was also said: "in" here means "idh" (when), as in His saying: ﴿And leave what remains of usury, if you are believers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 278]. In sum: the condition is placed after the answer. The rest read it with a fatha on the alif, as a causal clause, meaning: "because you are people who exceed the limits."

The second issue: al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: one says "daraba 'anhu" and "adraba 'anhu," meaning "he left it" and "he withheld from it." His saying ﴿ṣafḥan﴾ means "turning away." The original sense is that you turn away with the side of your neck. On this basis, His saying ﴿Shall We then turn away the Reminder from you ṣafḥan﴾ has the implied sense: "Shall We then withhold Our withholding from you?" or the implied sense: "Shall We then pardon you with a pardon?" They differed concerning the meaning of "the Reminder": it was said it means "Shall We then withhold from you the remembrance of Allah's punishment?" It was said: "Shall We withhold from you the admonitions and exhortations?" It was said: "Shall We withhold from you the Qur'an?" This is an interrogative in the form of denial, meaning: "We will not leave off this warning, this admonition, because you are people who exceed the limits." Qatadah said: if this Qur'an had been lifted when the first of this community rejected it, they would have perished, but Allah in His mercy repeated it to them and called them to it for twenty years. Having understood this, we say: this statement admits of two interpretations:

The first: mercy, meaning We will not abandon you despite your bad choice, but We will remind you and admonish you until you return to the right path.

The second: an emphasis on severity, meaning: do you think you will be left alone with what you desire? No, rather We will hold you to action, call you to the religion, and take you to account whenever you neglect the obligation and commit the abomination.

The third issue: the author of "al-Kashshaf" said: the fa' in His saying ﴿Shall We then turn away﴾ is for coordination with an omitted element, its implied sense being: "Shall We let you be, and then turn away the Reminder from you?"

* * *

Then Exalted Allah said: ﴿And how many a prophet did We send among the earlier peoples.﴾ ﴿Yet no prophet came to them but they mocked him.﴾ The meaning is that the custom of nations with the prophets who call them to the true religion is denial and mockery. Therefore you should not be distressed by your people's insistence on denial and mockery, because when a calamity becomes general, it becomes lighter.

* * *

Then Exalted Allah said: ﴿So We destroyed those who were stronger in might than these﴾, meaning that those earlier peoples to whom Allah sent the messengers were stronger in might than the Quraysh, that is, greater in number and vigor. Then He said: ﴿and the example of the earlier peoples has passed.﴾ The meaning is that the disbelievers of Mecca followed in disbelief and denial the path of those before them, so let them beware lest there descend upon them the same disgrace that descended upon them. We have set forth their example for them, as He said: ﴿And to each We set forth parables﴾ [al-Furqan: 39], and as in His saying: ﴿And you dwelt in the dwellings of those who wronged themselves﴾ [Ibrahim: 45] up to His saying ﴿and We set forth for you the parables.﴾ And Allah knows best.

The Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 43, verses 9–14 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And if you were to ask them, "Who created the heavens and the earth?" they would surely say, "They were created by the Mighty, the All-Knowing."﴾ ﴿Who made the earth for you a cradle and made for you therein roads that you may be guided.﴾ ﴿And who sent down from the sky water in measure, and We revived thereby a dead land. Thus you will be brought forth.﴾ ﴿And who created all the pairs and made for you of ships and cattle that which you ride,﴾ ﴿that you may sit upon their backs and then remember the favor of your Lord when you are seated upon them and say, "Exalted is He who has subjected these to us, and we could not have subdued them,"﴾ ﴿and indeed, to our Lord we will return.﴾

Know that the subject of the wasteful (al-musrifin), who are the polytheists, has already been mentioned, and the subject of the prophets has also already been mentioned. So His saying ﴿And if you were to ask them﴾ may refer back to the prophets, and it may refer back to the disbelievers, but the closer reference is to the disbelievers. Thus He, exalted is He, makes clear that they acknowledge that the creator of the heavens and the earth and what is between them is Allah, the Mighty, the Wise. The point is that, despite their acknowledging this meaning, they worship others alongside Him and deny His power to resurrect, and the report about them has already been given. Then He, exalted is He, began by indicating Himself through the mention of His creations, saying: ﴿Who made the earth for you a cradle﴾. Had this been part of the speech of the disbelievers, they would have had to say, "Who made the earth for us a cradle." Also, His saying in the midst of the speech ﴿and We revived thereby a dead land﴾ is connected only to the speech of Allah. Its parallel in human speech is that a man hears another man say: "The one who built this mosque is so-and-so the scholar," and the listener to this speech says: "The ascetic, the generous," as if that listener were saying: "I know him with praiseworthy attributes beyond what you know, so I will add to his description." Thus both descriptions come from two men about one man. Having understood the structure of the verse, we say: it indicates kinds of the attributes of Allah, exalted is He.

The first attribute: His being the creator of the heavens and the earth. The theologians (al-mutakallimun) have made clear that the first knowledge of Allah is knowledge that He is the originator of the world, its maker. For this reason the mention of Him as creator came first. This is complete only if we interpret creation (al-khalq) as bringing into existence and originating (al-ihdath wa al-ibda').

The second attribute: al-'Aziz (the Mighty), who is the Overpowering, and that by which He attains the capacity for overpowering is power (al-qudrah). It is as if al-'Aziz is an indication of the perfection of power.

The third attribute: al-'Alim (the All-Knowing), which is an indication of the perfection of knowledge. Know that when perfect knowledge and power are present, the one described by them is able to create all possible things. For this meaning, Allah, exalted is He, affirmed that He is described by these two attributes, and then based upon them the rest of the details.

The fourth attribute: His saying ﴿who made the earth for you a cradle﴾. We have mentioned in this book that the earth being a cradle came about because it is stationary and still, and because it is described by specific properties, by virtue of which it is possible to benefit from it in agriculture, building dwellings, and in its concealing the faults of the living and the dead. And since the cradle is the place of rest for the infant, He made the earth a cradle because of the abundance of rests in it.

The fifth attribute: His saying ﴿and made for you therein roads﴾. The point is that people's benefit is only complete if each person is able to travel from one land to another and from one region to another. Had Allah, exalted is He, not prepared those roads and placed upon them special signs, this benefit would not have been achieved.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿that you may be guided﴾, meaning: the purpose of placing the roads is that you attain the capacity for being guided. The second meaning: that you may be guided to the truth in religion.

The sixth attribute: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And who sent down from the sky water in measure, and We revived thereby a dead land﴾. Here there are discussions:

The first: the apparent meaning of this verse requires that water descends from the sky. Is the matter so, or is it said that it descends from the clouds, and it is called "descending from the sky" because everything that raises above you is a sky? This discussion has already been mentioned in full detail.

The second: His saying "in measure" (bi-qadar), meaning that it descends from the sky only in the measure that the people of that area need, without excess or deficiency, not as He sent down upon the people of Noah without measure until He drowned them, but in measure so that it is a means of livelihood for you and your livestock.

The third: His saying ﴿We revived thereby a dead land﴾, meaning empty of vegetation, and We revived it, and this is al-inshar (the reviving).

* * *

Then He said: ﴿Thus you will be brought forth﴾, meaning: just as this proof indicates the power and wisdom of Allah, so it indicates His power to resurrect and to the Resurrection. The aspect of the comparison is that He makes them living after death, like this land which was revived after it had been dead. Some have said: rather, the aspect of the comparison is that He restores them and brings them forth from the earth with water like semen, just as the earth grows by the water of rain. This view is weak, because the apparent wording contains only the affirmation of resurrection alone, not this additional meaning.

The seventh attribute: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And who created all the pairs﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: "The pairs are the kinds and types, such as sweet and sour, white and black, male and female." Some of the verifiers said: everything other than Allah is a pair, such as above and below, right and left, front and back, past and future, essences and attributes, summer and winter, spring and autumn. That they are pairs indicates that they are possible in their essences, originated, preceded by non-existence. As for the Truth, glorified is He, He is the Singular, transcendent above opposite, equal, counterpart, and helper. For this reason He, glorified is He, said: ﴿And who created all the pairs﴾, meaning: everything that is a pair is created, which indicates that its Creator is absolutely singular, transcendent above pairing. I also say: the scholars of the science of calculation have made clear that the single is superior to the pair in several respects:

The first: the least number of pairs is two, and this is found only when two units are present. So the pair needs the single, while the single, which is the unit, is independent of the pair, and the independent is superior to the one in need.

The second: the pair admits division into two equal parts, while the single is that which does not admit division. Admitting division is being affected and influenced, and not admitting it is strength, vigor, and resistance. So the single is superior to the pair.

The third: an odd number must have one of its two parts a pair and the other a single, so the odd number contains both the pair and the single together. As for the even number, each of its two parts must be a pair, and that which contains two parts is superior to that which is not so.

The fourth: pairing is an expression of each of its two parts being equal to the other part in essence, attributes, and quantity. And if whatever perfection is attained by one is also attained by its counterpart, then it is not perfect in an absolute sense. As for the single, singularity belongs to it specifically and not to anything else or to its like, so its perfection belongs to it alone and not to another, and so it is superior.

The fifth: the pair necessarily has each of its two parts sharing some matters with the other part and differing from it in other matters, and that by which they share is other than that by which they differ. So every pair is two things possible in their own essences, and everything possible is in need. Thus it is established that pairing is the source of poverty and need. As for singularity, it is the source of self-sufficiency and independence, because the number needs each one of those units, while each one of those units is independent of that number. Thus it is established that pairs are possible, originated, and created, and that the single is the one who subsists by Himself, independent by His own self, free of all that is other than Him. For this reason He, glorified is He, said: ﴿And who created all the pairs﴾.

The eighth attribute: His saying ﴿and made for you of ships and cattle that which you ride﴾. This is because travel is either sea travel or land travel. As for sea travel, the carrier is the ship, and as for land travel, the carrier is the cattle. Here there are two questions:

The first question: why did He not say "upon them" (ʿalayha)? They answered this in several ways:

The first: Abu 'Ubayda said: the masculine form is due to the word "ma" (what), and the sense is: "what you ride."

The second: al-Farra' said: He attributed "backs" (zuhur) to a singular noun that has the sense of a plural, like "army" and "troops," and for this reason He used the masculine and plural form for "backs."

The third: this feminine is not a true feminine, so the wording may differ in it, as one says: "Among the women there is one who agrees with you."

The second question: it is said: they ride the cattle, and they ride in the ships, and He has mentioned both kinds, so how did He say "you ride"? The answer: the transitive verb without an intermediary was given precedence, because of its strength, over the transitive verb with an intermediary.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿that you may sit upon their backs and then remember the favor of your Lord when you are seated upon them﴾. The meaning of remembering the favor of Allah is that they remember it in their hearts, and that remembrance is to know that Allah, exalted is He, created the surface of the sea, created the winds, and created the body of the ship in a manner by which a person is able to steer this ship in whatever direction he wishes and intends. So when they recall that the creation of the sea, the creation of the winds, and the creation of the ship in these forms, receptive to human manipulation and movement, is not by the management of that human, but is by the management of the Wise, the All-Knowing, the Powerful, they know that this is a great favor from Allah, exalted is He, and this moves them to submission and obedience to Him, exalted is He, and to occupying themselves with gratitude for His favors, which have no end.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿and say, "Exalted is He who has subjected this to us, and we could not have subdued it"﴾.

And know that He, exalted is He, designated a specific remembrance for boarding a ship, which is His saying, ﴿In the name of God is its course and its mooring﴾ [Hud: 41]. He designated another remembrance for riding livestock, which is His saying, ﴿Glory be to the One who subjected this to us﴾. And at the entering of dwellings He mentioned another remembrance, which is His saying, ﴿My Lord, cause me to land at a blessed landing, and You are the best of those who bring to land﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 29]. The clarification of this matter is that the beast a person rides must be far stronger than a person, and it has no intellect that guides it to obey the person. Rather, He, glory be to Him, created that animal in specific forms in its outward creation, and through its inward creation this benefit is obtained from it. As for its outward creation: it walks on four legs, so its back is like a place where a person can comfortably settle. As for its inward creation: despite its great strength, God, glory be to Him, created it in such a way that it becomes submissive to the person and subjected to him. So when a person reflects on these wonders and plunges with his intellect into the seas of these secrets, his amazement at that overpowering power and boundless wisdom grows greatly, and he must say, ﴿Glory be to the One who subjected this to us, and we could not have subdued it﴾.

Abu 'Ubayda said: "Fulan muqrin li-fulan" means he is capable of controlling him (ḍābiṭ lahu). Al-Wahidi said: It seems its derivation is from your saying "ḍaraba lahu qarnan" (he set up a rival to him), and the meaning of "anā qirnun li-fulan" (I am a match for so-and-so) is that I am his equal in strength. So the meaning is that we do not have, in strength and capacity, the ability to subdue this beast and the ship and to control them. Glory be to Him who subjected them to us by His knowledge, His wisdom, and the perfection of His power.

The author of the "al-Kashshaf" narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that: "When he placed his feet in the stirrups, he would say, 'In the name of God.' Then when he was seated firmly upon the beast, he would say, 'Praise be to God for every condition. Glory be to the One who subjected this to us, and we were not capable of it, and to our Lord we will surely return.'" Al-Qadi, in his "Tafsir," narrated from Abu Makhlad that al-Hasan ibn 'Ali, peace be upon them both, saw a man who had mounted a beast, and he said, "Glory be to the One who subjected this to us." He said to him, "This is not what you were commanded. You were commanded to say: Praise be to God who guided us to Islam; praise be to God who bestowed upon us Muhammad (ﷺ); and praise be to God who made us the best nation brought forth for mankind." Then you say, "Glory be to the One who subjected this to us."

It is also narrated from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) that: "When he travelled and mounted his riding beast, he would say 'Allahu akbar' three times, then say, 'Glory be to the One who subjected this to us,' then say: 'O God, I ask You in this journey of mine for righteousness and piety, and for deeds that please You. O God, make this journey easy for us and fold the distance of the earth for us. O God, You are the companion on the journey and the successor over the family. O God, accompany us on our journey and be our successor over our family.' And when he returned to his family, he would say: 'Returning, repenting, worshipping, and praising our Lord.'"

The author of "al-Kashshaf" said: This verse indicates against the view of the al-Mujbira (the determinists) in several respects.

The first: He, exalted is He, said, ﴿so that you may sit firm upon their backs and then remember the favour of your Lord﴾. He mentioned it with the particle "li" (so that), and this indicates that He intended this act from us. This indicates the invalidity of their claim that He intended disbelief from them and intended persistence in denial.

The second: His saying ﴿so that you may sit firm﴾ indicates that His act is caused by purposes (ta'lil bil-aghrad).

The third: He, exalted is He, made clear that the creation of these animals with these natures was only for the purpose that gratitude would proceed from the servant. If the act of the servant were an act of God, exalted is He, then the meaning of the verse would be: "I created these animals in order that I might create 'Glory be to God' on the tongue of the servant." This is false, because He is capable of creating this utterance on his tongue without these intermediaries.

Know that the discussion of these aspects is well known, so there is no benefit in repeating it.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said, ﴿And indeed to our Lord we will surely return﴾. Know that the connection of this statement with what precedes it is that boarding a ship is in a state of danger of destruction, for a ship often breaks and a person perishes. The rider of a beast is likewise, for a beast may encounter incidents that cause the death of its rider. Since this is so, riding a ship or a beast exposes the soul to destruction. Therefore the rider must remember the matter of death and be certain that he is surely destined to perish and that he will return to God, exalted is He, and cannot escape from His decree and His destiny. Thus, if that feared outcome befalls him, he will have already prepared himself for death.

[p. 172]

The Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 43, verses 9–14 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And if you were to ask them, "Who created the heavens and the earth?" they would surely say, "They were created by the Mighty, the All-Knowing."﴾ ﴿Who made the earth for you a cradle and made for you therein roads that you may be guided.﴾ ﴿And who sent down from the sky water in measure, and We revived thereby a dead land. Thus you will be brought forth.﴾ ﴿And who created all the pairs and made for you of ships and cattle that which you ride,﴾ ﴿that you may sit upon their backs and then remember the favor of your Lord when you are seated upon them and say, "Exalted is He who has subjected these to us, and we could not have subdued them,"﴾ ﴿and indeed, to our Lord we will return.﴾

Know that the subject of the wasteful (al-musrifin), who are the polytheists, has already been mentioned, and the subject of the prophets has also already been mentioned. So His saying ﴿And if you were to ask them﴾ may refer back to the prophets, and it may refer back to the disbelievers, but the closer reference is to the disbelievers. The third attribute: al-'Alim (the All-Knowing), which is an indication of the perfection of knowledge. The fourth attribute: His saying ﴿who made the earth for you a cradle﴾. And since the cradle is the place of rest for the infant, He made the earth a cradle because of the abundance of rests in it.

The fifth attribute: His saying ﴿and made for you therein roads﴾. The point is that people's benefit is only complete if each person is able to travel from one land to another and from one region to another. Had Allah, exalted is He, not prepared those roads and placed upon them special signs, this benefit would not have been achieved.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿that you may be guided﴾, meaning: the purpose of placing the roads is that you attain the capacity for being guided. The second meaning: that you may be guided to the truth in religion.

The first: the apparent meaning of this verse requires that water descends from the sky. Is the matter so, or is it said that it descends from the clouds, and it is called "descending from the sky" because everything that raises above you is a sky? This discussion has already been mentioned in full detail.

The second: His saying "in measure" (bi-qadar), meaning that it descends from the sky only in the measure that the people of that area need, without excess or deficiency, not as He sent down upon the people of Noah without measure until He drowned them, but in measure so that it is a means of livelihood for you and your livestock.

The third: His saying ﴿We revived thereby a dead land﴾, meaning empty of vegetation, and We revived it, and this is al-inshar (the reviving).

* * *

Then He said: ﴿Thus you will be brought forth﴾, meaning: just as this proof indicates the power and wisdom of Allah, so it indicates His power to resurrect and to the Resurrection. The aspect of the comparison is that He makes them living after death, like this land which was revived after it had been dead. Some have said: rather, the aspect of the comparison is that He restores them and brings them forth from the earth with water like semen, just as the earth grows by the water of rain. This view is weak, because the apparent wording contains only the affirmation of resurrection alone, not this additional meaning.

The first: the least number of pairs is two, and this is found only when two units are present. So the pair needs the single, while the single, which is the unit, is independent of the pair, and the independent is superior to the one in need.

The second: the pair admits division into two equal parts, while the single is that which does not admit division. Admitting division is being affected and influenced, and not admitting it is strength, vigor, and resistance. So the single is superior to the pair.

The third: an odd number must have one of its two parts a pair and the other a single, so the odd number contains both the pair and the single together. As for the even number, each of its two parts must be a pair, and that which contains two parts is superior to that which is not so.

The fourth: pairing is an expression of each of its two parts being equal to the other part in essence, attributes, and quantity. And if whatever perfection is attained by one is also attained by its counterpart, then it is not perfect in an absolute sense. As for the single, singularity belongs to it specifically and not to anything else or to its like, so its perfection belongs to it alone and not to another, and so it is superior.

The fifth: the pair necessarily has each of its two parts sharing some matters with the other part and differing from it in other matters, and that by which they share is other than that by which they differ. So every pair is two things possible in their own essences, and everything possible is in need. Thus it is established that pairing is the source of poverty and need. As for singularity, it is the source of self-sufficiency and independence, because the number needs each one of those units, while each one of those units is independent of that number. Thus it is established that pairs are possible, originated, and created, and that the single is the one who subsists by Himself, independent by His own self, free of all that is other than Him. For this reason He, glorified is He, said: ﴿And who created all the pairs﴾.

The first: Abu 'Ubayda said: the masculine form is due to the word "ma" (what), and the sense is: "what you ride."

The second: al-Farra' said: He attributed "backs" (zuhur) to a singular noun that has the sense of a plural, like "army" and "troops," and for this reason He used the masculine and plural form for "backs."

* * *

* * *

Rather, He, glory be to Him, created that animal in specific forms in its outward creation, and through its inward creation this benefit is obtained from it. As for its outward creation: it walks on four legs, so its back is like a place where a person can comfortably settle. As for its inward creation: despite its great strength, God, glory be to Him, created it in such a way that it becomes submissive to the person and subjected to him. Glory be to Him who subjected them to us by His knowledge, His wisdom, and the perfection of His power.

He said to him, "This is not what you were commanded. You were commanded to say: Praise be to God who guided us to Islam; praise be to God who bestowed upon us Muhammad (ﷺ); and praise be to God who made us the best nation brought forth for mankind." Then you say, "Glory be to the One who subjected this to us."

It is also narrated from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) that: "When he travelled and mounted his riding beast, he would say 'Allahu akbar' three times, then say, 'Glory be to the One who subjected this to us,' then say: 'O God, I ask You in this journey of mine for righteousness and piety, and for deeds that please You. O God, make this journey easy for us and fold the distance of the earth for us. O God, You are the companion on the journey and the successor over the family. O God, accompany us on our journey and be our successor over our family.' And when he returned to his family, he would say: 'Returning, repenting, worshipping, and praising our Lord.'"

The first: He, exalted is He, said, ﴿so that you may sit firm upon their backs and then remember the favour of your Lord﴾. He mentioned it with the particle "li" (so that), and this indicates that He intended this act from us. This indicates the invalidity of their claim that He intended disbelief from them and intended persistence in denial.

The second: His saying ﴿so that you may sit firm﴾ indicates that His act is caused by purposes (ta'lil bil-aghrad).

The third: He, exalted is He, made clear that the creation of these animals with these natures was only for the purpose that gratitude would proceed from the servant. If the act of the servant were an act of God, exalted is He, then the meaning of the verse would be: "I created these animals in order that I might create 'Glory be to God' on the tongue of the servant." This is false, because He is capable of creating this utterance on his tongue without these intermediaries.

Know that the discussion of these aspects is well known, so there is no benefit in repeating it.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said, ﴿And indeed to our Lord we will surely return﴾. The rider of a beast is likewise, for a beast may encounter incidents that cause the death of its rider. Since this is so, riding a ship or a beast exposes the soul to destruction. Therefore the rider must remember the matter of death and be certain that he is surely destined to perish and that he will return to God, exalted is He, and cannot escape from His decree and His destiny. Thus, if that feared outcome befalls him, he will have already prepared himself for death.

You were commanded to say: Praise be to God who guided us to Islam; praise be to God who bestowed upon us Muhammad (ﷺ); and praise be to God who made us the best nation brought forth for mankind." Then you say, "Glory be to the One who subjected this to us."

It is also narrated from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) that: "When he travelled and mounted his riding beast, he would say 'Allahu akbar' three times, then say, 'Glory be to the One who subjected this to us,' then say: 'O God, I ask You in this journey of mine for righteousness and piety, and for deeds that please You. O God, make this journey easy for us and fold the distance of the earth for us. O God, You are the companion on the journey and the successor over the family. The first: He, exalted is He, said, ﴿so that you may sit firm upon their backs and then remember the favour of your Lord﴾. He mentioned it with the particle "li" (so that), and this indicates that He intended this act from us. This indicates the invalidity of their claim that He intended disbelief from them and intended persistence in denial.

The second: His saying ﴿so that you may sit firm﴾ indicates that His act is caused by purposes (ta'lil bil-aghrad).

The third: He, exalted is He, made clear that the creation of these animals with these natures was only for the purpose that gratitude would proceed from the servant. If the act of the servant were an act of God, exalted is He, then the meaning of the verse would be: "I created these animals in order that I might create 'Glory be to God' on the tongue of the servant." This is false, because He is capable of creating this utterance on his tongue without these intermediaries.

Know that the discussion of these aspects is well known, so there is no benefit in repeating it.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said, ﴿And indeed to our Lord we will surely return﴾. He mentioned it with the particle "li" (so that), and this indicates that He intended this act from us. This indicates the invalidity of their claim that He intended disbelief from them and intended persistence in denial.

The second: His saying ﴿so that you may sit firm﴾ indicates that His act is caused by purposes (ta'lil bil-aghrad).

The third: He, exalted is He, made clear that the creation of these animals with these natures was only for the purpose that gratitude would proceed from the servant. If the act of the servant were an act of God, exalted is He, then the meaning of the verse would be: "I created these animals in order that I might create 'Glory be to God' on the tongue of the servant." This is false, because He is capable of creating this utterance on his tongue without these intermediaries.

Know that the discussion of these aspects is well known, so there is no benefit in repeating it.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said, ﴿And indeed to our Lord we will surely return﴾. Know that the connection of this statement with what precedes it is that boarding a ship is in a state of danger of destruction, for a ship often breaks and a person perishes. The rider of a beast is likewise, for a beast may encounter incidents that cause the death of its rider. Since this is so, riding a ship or a beast exposes the soul to destruction. Therefore the rider must remember the matter of death and be certain that he is surely destined to perish and that he will return to God, exalted is He, and cannot escape from His decree and His destiny. Thus, if that feared outcome befalls him, he will have already prepared himself for death.

[p. 172]

The Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 43, verses 9–14 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And if you were to ask them, "Who created the heavens and the earth?" they would surely say, "They were created by the Mighty, the All-Knowing."﴾ ﴿Who made the earth for you a cradle and made for you therein roads that you may be guided.﴾ ﴿And who sent down from the sky water in measure, and We revived thereby a dead land. Thus you will be brought forth.﴾ ﴿And who created all the pairs and made for you of ships and cattle that which you ride,﴾ ﴿that you may sit upon their backs and then remember the favor of your Lord when you are seated upon them and say, "Exalted is He who has subjected these to us, and we could not have subdued them,"﴾ ﴿and indeed, to our Lord we will return.﴾

Know that the subject of the wasteful (al-musrifin), who are the polytheists, has already been mentioned, and the subject of the prophets has also already been mentioned. So His saying ﴿And if you were to ask them﴾ may refer back to the prophets, and it may refer back to the disbelievers, but the closer reference is to the disbelievers. Thus He, exalted is He, makes clear that they acknowledge that the creator of the heavens and the earth and what is between them is Allah, the Mighty, the Wise. The point is that, despite their acknowledging this meaning, they worship others alongside Him and deny His power to resurrect, and the report about them has already been given. Then He, exalted is He, began by indicating Himself through the mention of His creations, saying: ﴿Who made the earth for you a cradle﴾. Had this been part of the speech of the disbelievers, they would have had to say, "Who made the earth for us a cradle." Also, His saying in the midst of the speech ﴿and We revived thereby a dead land﴾ is connected only to the speech of Allah. Its parallel in human speech is that a man hears another man say: "The one who built this mosque is so-and-so the scholar," and the listener to this speech says: "The ascetic, the generous," as if that listener were saying: "I know him with praiseworthy attributes beyond what you know, so I will add to his description." Thus both descriptions come from two men about one man. Having understood the structure of the verse, we say: it indicates kinds of the attributes of Allah, exalted is He.

The first attribute: His being the creator of the heavens and the earth. The theologians (al-mutakallimun) have made clear that the first knowledge of Allah is knowledge that He is the originator of the world, its maker. For this reason the mention of Him as creator came first. This is complete only if we interpret creation (al-khalq) as bringing into existence and originating (al-ihdath wa al-ibda').

The second attribute: al-'Aziz (the Mighty), who is the Overpowering, and that by which He attains the capacity for overpowering is power (al-qudrah). It is as if al-'Aziz is an indication of the perfection of power.

The third attribute: al-'Alim (the All-Knowing), which is an indication of the perfection of knowledge. Know that when perfect knowledge and power are present, the one described by them is able to create all possible things. For this meaning, Allah, exalted is He, affirmed that He is described by these two attributes, and then based upon them the rest of the details.

The fourth attribute: His saying ﴿who made the earth for you a cradle﴾. We have mentioned in this book that the earth being a cradle came about because it is stationary and still, and because it is described by specific properties, by virtue of which it is possible to benefit from it in agriculture, building dwellings, and in its concealing the faults of the living and the dead. And since the cradle is the place of rest for the infant, He made the earth a cradle because of the abundance of rests in it.

The fifth attribute: His saying ﴿and made for you therein roads﴾. The point is that people's benefit is only complete if each person is able to travel from one land to another and from one region to another. Had Allah, exalted is He, not prepared those roads and placed upon them special signs, this benefit would not have been achieved.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿that you may be guided﴾, meaning: the purpose of placing the roads is that you attain the capacity for being guided. The second meaning: that you may be guided to the truth in religion.

The sixth attribute: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And who sent down from the sky water in measure, and We revived thereby a dead land﴾. Here there are discussions:

The first: the apparent meaning of this verse requires that water descends from the sky. Is the matter so, or is it said that it descends from the clouds, and it is called "descending from the sky" because everything that raises above you is a sky? This discussion has already been mentioned in full detail.

The second: His saying "in measure" (bi-qadar), meaning that it descends from the sky only in the measure that the people of that area need, without excess or deficiency, not as He sent down upon the people of Noah without measure until He drowned them, but in measure so that it is a means of livelihood for you and your livestock.

The third: His saying ﴿We revived thereby a dead land﴾, meaning empty of vegetation, and We revived it, and this is al-inshar (the reviving).

* * *

Then He said: ﴿Thus you will be brought forth﴾, meaning: just as this proof indicates the power and wisdom of Allah, so it indicates His power to resurrect and to the Resurrection. The aspect of the comparison is that He makes them living after death, like this land which was revived after it had been dead. Some have said: rather, the aspect of the comparison is that He restores them and brings them forth from the earth with water like semen, just as the earth grows by the water of rain. This view is weak, because the apparent wording contains only the affirmation of resurrection alone, not this additional meaning.

The seventh attribute: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And who created all the pairs﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: "The pairs are the kinds and types, such as sweet and sour, white and black, male and female." Some of the verifiers said: everything other than Allah is a pair, such as above and below, right and left, front and back, past and future, essences and attributes, summer and winter, spring and autumn. That they are pairs indicates that they are possible in their essences, originated, preceded by non-existence. As for the Truth, glorified is He, He is the Singular, transcendent above opposite, equal, counterpart, and helper. For this reason He, glorified is He, said: ﴿And who created all the pairs﴾, meaning: everything that is a pair is created, which indicates that its Creator is absolutely singular, transcendent above pairing. I also say: the scholars of the science of calculation have made clear that the single is superior to the pair in several respects:

The first: the least number of pairs is two, and this is found only when two units are present. So the pair needs the single, while the single, which is the unit, is independent of the pair, and the independent is superior to the one in need.

The second: the pair admits division into two equal parts, while the single is that which does not admit division. Admitting division is being affected and influenced, and not admitting it is strength, vigor, and resistance. So the single is superior to the pair.

The third: an odd number must have one of its two parts a pair and the other a single, so the odd number contains both the pair and the single together. As for the even number, each of its two parts must be a pair, and that which contains two parts is superior to that which is not so.

The fourth: pairing is an expression of each of its two parts being equal to the other part in essence, attributes, and quantity. And if whatever perfection is attained by one is also attained by its counterpart, then it is not perfect in an absolute sense. As for the single, singularity belongs to it specifically and not to anything else or to its like, so its perfection belongs to it alone and not to another, and so it is superior.

The fifth: the pair necessarily has each of its two parts sharing some matters with the other part and differing from it in other matters, and that by which they share is other than that by which they differ. So every pair is two things possible in their own essences, and everything possible is in need. Thus it is established that pairing is the source of poverty and need. As for singularity, it is the source of self-sufficiency and independence, because the number needs each one of those units, while each one of those units is independent of that number. Thus it is established that pairs are possible, originated, and created, and that the single is the one who subsists by Himself, independent by His own self, free of all that is other than Him. For this reason He, glorified is He, said: ﴿And who created all the pairs﴾.

The eighth attribute: His saying ﴿and made for you of ships and cattle that which you ride﴾. This is because travel is either sea travel or land travel. As for sea travel, the carrier is the ship, and as for land travel, the carrier is the cattle. Here there are two questions:

The first question: why did He not say "upon them" (ʿalayha)? They answered this in several ways:

The first: Abu 'Ubayda said: the masculine form is due to the word "ma" (what), and the sense is: "what you ride."

The second: al-Farra' said: He attributed "backs" (zuhur) to a singular noun that has the sense of a plural, like "army" and "troops," and for this reason He used the masculine and plural form for "backs."

The third: this feminine is not a true feminine, so the wording may differ in it, as one says: "Among the women there is one who agrees with you."

The second question: it is said: they ride the cattle, and they ride in the ships, and He has mentioned both kinds, so how did He say "you ride"? The answer: the transitive verb without an intermediary was given precedence, because of its strength, over the transitive verb with an intermediary.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿that you may sit upon their backs and then remember the favor of your Lord when you are seated upon them﴾. The meaning of remembering the favor of Allah is that they remember it in their hearts, and that remembrance is to know that Allah, exalted is He, created the surface of the sea, created the winds, and created the body of the ship in a manner by which a person is able to steer this ship in whatever direction he wishes and intends. So when they recall that the creation of the sea, the creation of the winds, and the creation of the ship in these forms, receptive to human manipulation and movement, is not by the management of that human, but is by the management of the Wise, the All-Knowing, the Powerful, they know that this is a great favor from Allah, exalted is He, and this moves them to submission and obedience to Him, exalted is He, and to occupying themselves with gratitude for His favors, which have no end.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿and say, "Exalted is He who has subjected this to us, and we could not have subdued it"﴾.

And know that He, exalted is He, designated a specific remembrance for boarding a ship, which is His saying, ﴿In the name of God is its course and its mooring﴾ [Hud: 41]. He designated another remembrance for riding livestock, which is His saying, ﴿Glory be to the One who subjected this to us﴾. And at the entering of dwellings He mentioned another remembrance, which is His saying, ﴿My Lord, cause me to land at a blessed landing, and You are the best of those who bring to land﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 29]. The clarification of this matter is that the beast a person rides must be far stronger than a person, and it has no intellect that guides it to obey the person. Rather, He, glory be to Him, created that animal in specific forms in its outward creation, and through its inward creation this benefit is obtained from it. As for its outward creation: it walks on four legs, so its back is like a place where a person can comfortably settle. As for its inward creation: despite its great strength, God, glory be to Him, created it in such a way that it becomes submissive to the person and subjected to him. So when a person reflects on these wonders and plunges with his intellect into the seas of these secrets, his amazement at that overpowering power and boundless wisdom grows greatly, and he must say, ﴿Glory be to the One who subjected this to us, and we could not have subdued it﴾.

Abu 'Ubayda said: "Fulan muqrin li-fulan" means he is capable of controlling him (ḍābiṭ lahu). Al-Wahidi said: It seems its derivation is from your saying "ḍaraba lahu qarnan" (he set up a rival to him), and the meaning of "anā qirnun li-fulan" (I am a match for so-and-so) is that I am his equal in strength. So the meaning is that we do not have, in strength and capacity, the ability to subdue this beast and the ship and to control them. Glory be to Him who subjected them to us by His knowledge, His wisdom, and the perfection of His power.

The author of the "al-Kashshaf" narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that: "When he placed his feet in the stirrups, he would say, 'In the name of God.' Then when he was seated firmly upon the beast, he would say, 'Praise be to God for every condition. Glory be to the One who subjected this to us, and we were not capable of it, and to our Lord we will surely return.'" Al-Qadi, in his "Tafsir," narrated from Abu Makhlad that al-Hasan ibn 'Ali, peace be upon them both, saw a man who had mounted a beast, and he said, "Glory be to the One who subjected this to us." He said to him, "This is not what you were commanded. You were commanded to say: Praise be to God who guided us to Islam; praise be to God who bestowed upon us Muhammad (ﷺ); and praise be to God who made us the best nation brought forth for mankind." Then you say, "Glory be to the One who subjected this to us."

It is also narrated from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) that: "When he travelled and mounted his riding beast, he would say 'Allahu akbar' three times, then say, 'Glory be to the One who subjected this to us,' then say: 'O God, I ask You in this journey of mine for righteousness and piety, and for deeds that please You. O God, make this journey easy for us and fold the distance of the earth for us. O God, You are the companion on the journey and the successor over the family. O God, accompany us on our journey and be our successor over our family.' And when he returned to his family, he would say: 'Returning, repenting, worshipping, and praising our Lord.'"

The author of "al-Kashshaf" said: This verse indicates against the view of the al-Mujbira (the determinists) in several respects.

The first: He, exalted is He, said, ﴿so that you may sit firm upon their backs and then remember the favour of your Lord﴾. He mentioned it with the particle "li" (so that), and this indicates that He intended this act from us. This indicates the invalidity of their claim that He intended disbelief from them and intended persistence in denial.

The second: His saying ﴿so that you may sit firm﴾ indicates that His act is caused by purposes (ta'lil bil-aghrad).

The third: He, exalted is He, made clear that the creation of these animals with these natures was only for the purpose that gratitude would proceed from the servant. If the act of the servant were an act of God, exalted is He, then the meaning of the verse would be: "I created these animals in order that I might create 'Glory be to God' on the tongue of the servant." This is false, because He is capable of creating this utterance on his tongue without these intermediaries.

Know that the discussion of these aspects is well known, so there is no benefit in repeating it.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said, ﴿And indeed to our Lord we will surely return﴾. Know that the connection of this statement with what precedes it is that boarding a ship is in a state of danger of destruction, for a ship often breaks and a person perishes. The rider of a beast is likewise, for a beast may encounter incidents that cause the death of its rider. Since this is so, riding a ship or a beast exposes the soul to destruction. Therefore the rider must remember the matter of death and be certain that he is surely destined to perish and that he will return to God, exalted is He, and cannot escape from His decree and His destiny. Thus, if that feared outcome befalls him, he will have already prepared himself for death.
