His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And when the son of Mary is cited as an example, behold, your people turn away from it. And they said, "Are our gods better, or is he?" They only cited it to you for argument. Indeed, they are a contentious people. He is only a servant upon whom We bestowed favor, and We made him an example for the Children of Israel. And if We willed, We would have made from among you angels to succeed on the earth. And indeed, he is a sign for the Hour, so do not be in doubt about it, and follow Me. This is a straight path. And let not Satan avert you; indeed, he is to you a clear enemy.﴾ 50

In the verse there are several issues.

First issue: Know that He Exalted mentioned many kinds of their disbelieving statements in this surah, and answered them with many aspects:

The first of them: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they have made for Him from His servants a portion﴾.

The second of them: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they have made the angels, who are the servants of the Most Merciful, females﴾.

The third of them: His saying: ﴿And they said, "Had the Most Merciful willed, we would not have worshipped them"﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 20].

Fourth: His saying, "And they say, 'Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a man from the two cities, a great one?'" (al-Zukhruf: 31).

Fifth: This is the verse we are now explaining. The wording of the verse indicates only that when the son of Mary was presented as an example, the people began to clamor and raise their voices. As for what that example was like and in what respect it was, the wording does not indicate it. The exegetes have mentioned several explanations for it, all of which are possible:

The first: When the disbelievers heard that the Christians worship Jesus, they said, "If they worship Jesus, then our gods are better than Jesus." They only said this because they were worshipping the angels.

The second: It is narrated that when His saying, Exalted is He, "Indeed, you and what you worship besides Allah are the fuel of Hell" (al-Anbiya: 98) was revealed, Abdullah ibn al-Zib'ara said, "Is this specific to us and our gods, or is it for all nations?" The Prophet ﷺ said, "Rather, it is for all nations." He said, "I have defeated you, by the Lord of the Ka'bah! Do you not claim that Jesus son of Mary is a prophet, and you praise him and his mother with goodness? I know that the Christians worship them both, and the Jews worship Uzayr, and the angels are worshipped. If these are in the Fire, then we are content that we and our gods be with them." The Prophet ﷺ fell silent, the people rejoiced, laughed and clamored. Then Allah, Exalted is He, revealed: "Indeed, those for whom the good has preceded from Us, those are kept far away from it" (al-Anbiya: 101). This verse was also revealed. The meaning: When Abdullah ibn al-Zib'ara presented Jesus "the son of Mary as an example" and disputed with the Messenger of Allah regarding the worship of the Christians of him,
page 190
"behold, your people" — Quraysh — "from it" — that is, from this example — "turn away" — that is, a clamor and uproar rises up from them in joy, disputation and laughter because of what they saw of the silencing of the Messenger of Allah. It is customary that when one of two opponents is silenced, the other opponent shows joy and clamor. "And they said, 'Are our gods better, or is he?'" meaning: our gods in your view are not better than Jesus, so if Jesus is among the fuel of Hell, the matter of our gods is even less.

The third explanation: When the Prophet ﷺ related that the Christians worshipped the Messiah and made him a god for themselves, the disbelievers of Makkah said, "Muhammad wants to make for us a god just as the Christians made the Messiah a god for themselves." Then, at this point, they said, "Are our gods better, or is he?" meaning: are our gods better, or Muhammad? They mentioned this because they said, "Muhammad calls us to worship himself, and our fathers claimed that it is obligatory to worship these idols. If one of these two matters is unavoidable, then worshipping these idols is preferable, because our fathers and forefathers agreed upon it, whereas Muhammad is accused in our affair of seeking to be worshipped." So occupation with worshipping idols was preferable. Then He, Exalted is He, clarified that we did not say that occupation with worshipping the Messiah is a good path; rather, it is false speech, for Jesus is nothing but a servant upon whom We bestowed favour. If the matter is so, then their doubt in their saying that Muhammad wants to command us to worship himself has been removed. These three explanations are such that each of them is possible in the wording of the verse.

Second issue: Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, al-Kisa'i and Abu Bakr from 'Asim read "yasuddun" with a dammah on the sad, which is the reading of 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, peace be upon him. The rest read it with a kasrah on the sad, which is the reading of Ibn 'Abbas. They differed: al-Kisa'i said, "They have the same meaning, like ya'rishun and ya'rushun, and ya'kifun and ya'kufun." Among them some distinguished: As for the reading with a dammah, it is from *al-sudud* (turning away), meaning because of this example they turn away from the truth and avoid it; as for the reading with a kasrah, its meaning is clamoring.

Third issue: 'Asim, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "a-alihatuna" as an interrogative with two hamzahs, the second being prolonged; the rest read it as an interrogative with one hamzah and a madd.

* * *

Then He, Exalted is He, said: "They did not present it to you except for disputation" (al-Zukhruf: 58), meaning: they did not present this example to you except for the sake of disputation and victory in speech, not seeking to distinguish truth from falsehood. "Rather, they are a contentious people" (al-Zukhruf: 58), exceeding in contention. This is because His saying, "Indeed, you and what you worship besides Allah" (al-Anbiya: 98), does not include the angels and Jesus. Its explanation is in several respects:

First: the word *ma* (what) does not at all include rational beings.

Second: the word *ma* is not explicit in universality, as evidenced by the fact that it is correct to add the words "all" and "some" to it, so one says: "Indeed, you and all that you worship besides Allah," or "Indeed, you and some of what you worship besides Allah."

Third: His saying, "Indeed, you and all that you worship besides Allah," or "and some of what you worship," is direct address, so perhaps there was no one among them who worshipped the Messiah or the angels.

Fourth: even granting that His saying, "Indeed, you and what you worship besides Allah," is general, the texts indicating the exaltation of the angels and Jesus are more specific than it, and the specific takes precedence over the general.

Fourth issue: Those who call for condemning disputation have held to this verse. However, we have mentioned in the explanation of His saying, "None dispute concerning the signs of Allah except those who disbelieve" (Ghafir: 4), that many verses indicate that disputation is praiseworthy and commendable. The way to reconcile is to direct those verses to disputation that establishes the truth, and to direct this verse to disputation that establishes falsehood.

* * *

Then He, Exalted is He, said: "He is only a servant upon whom We bestowed favour" (al-Zukhruf: 59), meaning: Jesus is nothing but a servant like other servants, upon whom We bestowed favour by making him a sign, creating him without a father as We created Adam, honouring him with prophethood, and making him a wondrous lesson, like a well-known proverb. "And had We willed" (al-Zukhruf: 60),
page 191
"We would have made from among you" — We would have produced from you, O men — "angels upon the earth succeeding" (al-Zukhruf: 60), as your children succeed you; just as We produced Jesus from a female without a male, so that you may know Our distinction by the overwhelming power, and so that you may know that the occurrence of begetting and being begotten among angels is a possible matter, while the Essence of Allah is exalted above that. "And indeed, he" — that is, Jesus — "is a sign of the Hour" (al-Zukhruf: 61), a condition of its portents by which it is known. The condition that indicates a thing is called a knowledge, because knowledge of it is obtained through it. Ibn 'Abbas read "la-'alamun," which means a sign. It was also read "lil-'ilm," and Ubayy read "la-dhikr." In a hadith: "Jesus will descend at a mountain pass in the holy land called Afiq, with a spear in his hand, and with it he will kill the Dajjal. He will come to Bayt al-Maqdis at the dawn prayer while the imam is leading them; the imam will draw back, and Jesus will move him forward and pray behind him according to the law of Muhammad ﷺ. Then he will kill the swine, break the cross, destroy the churches and synagogues, and kill the Christians except those who believe in him." "So do not be in doubt about it" (al-Zukhruf: 61), from *al-mirya*, which is doubt. "And follow Me" (al-Zukhruf: 61), follow My guidance and My law. "This is a straight path" (al-Zukhruf: 61), meaning: this to which I call you is a straight path. "And let not Satan avert you; indeed, he is to you a clear enemy" (al-Zukhruf: 62), whose enmity has become evident to you, because he is the one who expelled your father from the Garden and stripped from him the garment of light.

[Commentary of al-Razi, Mafatih al-Ghayb, on surah 43, verses 48–62 (part 1 of 2)]

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We indeed sent Moses with Our signs to Pharaoh and his chiefs, and he said, "I am a messenger of the Lord of the worlds." But when he brought them Our signs, behold, they laughed at them. And We did not show them any sign but it was greater than its fellow, and We seized them with punishment so that they might return.﴾ ﴿And they said, "O sorcerer, invoke your Lord for us by what He has covenanted with you. Indeed, we are guided."﴾ ﴿But when We removed the punishment from them, behold, they broke their word.﴾ ﴿And Pharaoh proclaimed among his people, saying, "O my people, is not the kingdom of Egypt mine, and these rivers flowing beneath me? Do you not see? Or am I better than this one who is contemptible and can hardly express himself? Why have bracelets of gold not been put upon him, or the angels not come with him in succession?"﴾ ﴿So he made his people feeble-minded, and they obeyed him. Indeed, they were a defiant people.﴾ ﴿And when they angered Us, We took vengeance upon them and drowned them all.﴾

In the verse there are several issues.

First issue: Know that the purpose of repeating the story of Moses, peace be upon him, and Pharaoh in this context is to confirm what was said earlier. This is because the disbelievers of Quraysh criticized the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ on the ground that he was poor, lacking wealth and status. So God Exalted explained that Moses, peace be upon him, after presenting the overpowering and dazzling miracles, about whose truth no sane person doubts, was met by Pharaoh with the same doubt that the disbelievers of Quraysh raised. He said: "I am rich, abounding in wealth and status. Do you not see that the kingdom of Egypt has come to me, and these rivers flow beneath me? As for Moses, he is poor and contemptible, and he has neither eloquence nor tongue. How can a poor man be a messenger from God to a great, wealthy king?" Thus it is established that this doubt which the disbelievers of Mecca raised, namely their saying ﴿Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a great man from the two cities?﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 31], was raised by Pharaoh against Moses in exactly the same words. Then We took vengeance upon them and drowned them. The purpose of mentioning this story is to confirm two matters:

One of them: that disbelievers and ignorant people always argue against the prophets with this feeble doubt, so it should be disregarded and not paid attention to.

The second: that Pharaoh, at the height of his worldly state, became humiliated and false, so the matter regarding your enemies will be likewise. Thus it is established that the purpose of repeating this story is not the very same story, but rather to confirm the answer to the aforementioned doubt. On this basis, this is not a retelling of the story at all. This is one of the finest investigations, and God knows best.

[Page 187]

Second issue, on interpreting the words: God mentioned that He sent Moses with His signs, namely the miracles that were with Moses, peace be upon him, to Pharaoh and his chiefs, that is, his people. Moses said, "I am a messenger of the Lord of the worlds." When he brought them those signs, behold, they laughed at them. It is said that when he cast down his staff and it became a serpent, then he took it and it returned to being a staff as it was, they laughed. And when he showed them the white hand, then it returned as it was, they laughed. If it is asked: how is it permissible to answer "lamma" (when) with "idha" (behold), which expresses sudden occurrence? We say: because the verb of sudden occurrence is implied with it; as if it were said: "When he brought them Our signs, they were suddenly at the time of their laughing."

Then He said: ﴿And We did not show them any sign but it was greater than its fellow.﴾ If it is asked: the apparent meaning of the words requires that each one be better than the one that follows, and that is impossible. We say: when the intention is to emphasize that each of those things reached the utmost degrees of excellence, this statement may be used in the sense that it is not unlikely, among people looking at them, that one says: "This is better than the second," and another says: "No, the second is better," and a third says: "No, the third is better." In that case each of those things is described as being better than the others.

Then God Exalted said: ﴿So We made them a precedent and an example﴾. "Salaf" is everything you have sent ahead of you of righteous deeds or loans, so it is a "salaf." Accordingly, al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: He says: "We made them those who go before, so that others may take warning from them", that is, We made them a precedent for the disbelievers of the nation of Muhammad, peace be upon him. And God knows best.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And when the son of Mary is cited as an example, behold, your people turn away from it. And they said, "Are our gods better, or is he?" They only cited it to you for argument. Indeed, they are a contentious people. He is only a servant upon whom We bestowed favor, and We made him an example for the Children of Israel. And if We willed, We would have made from among you angels to succeed on the earth. And indeed, he is a sign for the Hour, so do not be in doubt about it, and follow Me. This is a straight path. And let not Satan avert you; indeed, he is to you a clear enemy.﴾ 50

In the verse there are several issues.

First issue: Know that He Exalted mentioned many kinds of their disbelieving statements in this surah, and answered them with many aspects:

The first of them: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they have made for Him from His servants a portion﴾.

The second of them: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they have made the angels, who are the servants of the Most Merciful, females﴾.

The third of them: His saying: ﴿And they said, "Had the Most Merciful willed, we would not have worshipped them"﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 20].

Fourth: His saying, "And they say, 'Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a man from the two cities, a great one?'" (al-Zukhruf: 31).

Fifth: This is the verse we are now explaining. The wording of the verse indicates only that when the son of Mary was presented as an example, the people began to clamor and raise their voices. As for what that example was like and in what respect it was, the wording does not indicate it. The exegetes have mentioned several explanations for it, all of which are possible:

The first: When the disbelievers heard that the Christians worship Jesus, they said, "If they worship Jesus, then our gods are better than Jesus." They only said this because they were worshipping the angels.

The second: It is narrated that when His saying, Exalted is He, "Indeed, you and what you worship besides Allah are the fuel of Hell" (al-Anbiya: 98) was revealed, Abdullah ibn al-Zib'ara said, "Is this specific to us and our gods, or is it for all nations?" The Prophet ﷺ said, "Rather, it is for all nations." He said, "I have defeated you, by the Lord of the Ka'bah! Do you not claim that Jesus son of Mary is a prophet, and you praise him and his mother with goodness? I know that the Christians worship them both, and the Jews worship Uzayr, and the angels are worshipped. If these are in the Fire, then we are content that we and our gods be with them." The Prophet ﷺ fell silent, the people rejoiced, laughed and clamored. Then Allah, Exalted is He, revealed: "Indeed, those for whom the good has preceded from Us, those are kept far away from it" (al-Anbiya: 101). This verse was also revealed. The meaning: When Abdullah ibn al-Zib'ara presented Jesus "the son of Mary as an example" and disputed with the Messenger of Allah regarding the worship of the Christians of him,
page 190
"behold, your people" — Quraysh — "from it" — that is, from this example — "turn away" — that is, a clamor and uproar rises up from them in joy, disputation and laughter because of what they saw of the silencing of the Messenger of Allah. It is customary that when one of two opponents is silenced, the other opponent shows joy and clamor. "And they said, 'Are our gods better, or is he?'" meaning: our gods in your view are not better than Jesus, so if Jesus is among the fuel of Hell, the matter of our gods is even less.

The third explanation: When the Prophet ﷺ related that the Christians worshipped the Messiah and made him a god for themselves, the disbelievers of Makkah said, "Muhammad wants to make for us a god just as the Christians made the Messiah a god for themselves." Then, at this point, they said, "Are our gods better, or is he?" meaning: are our gods better, or Muhammad? They mentioned this because they said, "Muhammad calls us to worship himself, and our fathers claimed that it is obligatory to worship these idols. If one of these two matters is unavoidable, then worshipping these idols is preferable, because our fathers and forefathers agreed upon it, whereas Muhammad is accused in our affair of seeking to be worshipped." So occupation with worshipping idols was preferable. Then He, Exalted is He, clarified that we did not say that occupation with worshipping the Messiah is a good path; rather, it is false speech, for Jesus is nothing but a servant upon whom We bestowed favour. If the matter is so, then their doubt in their saying that Muhammad wants to command us to worship himself has been removed. These three explanations are such that each of them is possible in the wording of the verse.

Second issue: Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, al-Kisa'i and Abu Bakr from 'Asim read "yasuddun" with a dammah on the sad, which is the reading of 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, peace be upon him. The rest read it with a kasrah on the sad, which is the reading of Ibn 'Abbas. They differed: al-Kisa'i said, "They have the same meaning, like ya'rishun and ya'rushun, and ya'kifun and ya'kufun." Among them some distinguished: As for the reading with a dammah, it is from *al-sudud* (turning away), meaning because of this example they turn away from the truth and avoid it; as for the reading with a kasrah, its meaning is clamoring.

Third issue: 'Asim, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "a-alihatuna" as an interrogative with two hamzahs, the second being prolonged; the rest read it as an interrogative with one hamzah and a madd.

* * *

Then He, Exalted is He, said: "They did not present it to you except for disputation" (al-Zukhruf: 58), meaning: they did not present this example to you except for the sake of disputation and victory in speech, not seeking to distinguish truth from falsehood. "Rather, they are a contentious people" (al-Zukhruf: 58), exceeding in contention. This is because His saying, "Indeed, you and what you worship besides Allah" (al-Anbiya: 98), does not include the angels and Jesus. Its explanation is in several respects:

First: the word *ma* (what) does not at all include rational beings.

Second: the word *ma* is not explicit in universality, as evidenced by the fact that it is correct to add the words "all" and "some" to it, so one says: "Indeed, you and all that you worship besides Allah," or "Indeed, you and some of what you worship besides Allah."

Third: His saying, "Indeed, you and all that you worship besides Allah," or "and some of what you worship," is direct address, so perhaps there was no one among them who worshipped the Messiah or the angels.

Fourth: even granting that His saying, "Indeed, you and what you worship besides Allah," is general, the texts indicating the exaltation of the angels and Jesus are more specific than it, and the specific takes precedence over the general.

Fourth issue: Those who call for condemning disputation have held to this verse. However, we have mentioned in the explanation of His saying, "None dispute concerning the signs of Allah except those who disbelieve" (Ghafir: 4), that many verses indicate that disputation is praiseworthy and commendable. The way to reconcile is to direct those verses to disputation that establishes the truth, and to direct this verse to disputation that establishes falsehood.

* * *

Then He, Exalted is He, said: "He is only a servant upon whom We bestowed favour" (al-Zukhruf: 59), meaning: Jesus is nothing but a servant like other servants, upon whom We bestowed favour by making him a sign, creating him without a father as We created Adam, honouring him with prophethood, and making him a wondrous lesson, like a well-known proverb. "And had We willed" (al-Zukhruf: 60),
page 191
"We would have made from among you" — We would have produced from you, O men — "angels upon the earth succeeding" (al-Zukhruf: 60), as your children succeed you; just as We produced Jesus from a female without a male, so that you may know Our distinction by the overwhelming power, and so that you may know that the occurrence of begetting and being begotten among angels is a possible matter, while the Essence of Allah is exalted above that. "And indeed, he" — that is, Jesus — "is a sign of the Hour" (al-Zukhruf: 61), a condition of its portents by which it is known. The condition that indicates a thing is called a knowledge, because knowledge of it is obtained through it. Ibn 'Abbas read "la-'alamun," which means a sign. It was also read "lil-'ilm," and Ubayy read "la-dhikr." In a hadith: "Jesus will descend at a mountain pass in the holy land called Afiq, with a spear in his hand, and with it he will kill the Dajjal. He will come to Bayt al-Maqdis at the dawn prayer while the imam is leading them; the imam will draw back, and Jesus will move him forward and pray behind him according to the law of Muhammad ﷺ. Then he will kill the swine, break the cross, destroy the churches and synagogues, and kill the Christians except those who believe in him." "So do not be in doubt about it" (al-Zukhruf: 61), from *al-mirya*, which is doubt. "And follow Me" (al-Zukhruf: 61), follow My guidance and My law. "This is a straight path" (al-Zukhruf: 61), meaning: this to which I call you is a straight path. "And let not Satan avert you; indeed, he is to you a clear enemy" (al-Zukhruf: 62), whose enmity has become evident to you, because he is the one who expelled your father from the Garden and stripped from him the garment of light.

[Commentary of al-Razi, Mafatih al-Ghayb, on surah 43, verses 48–62 (part 1 of 2)]

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We indeed sent Moses with Our signs to Pharaoh and his chiefs, and he said, "I am a messenger of the Lord of the worlds." But when he brought them Our signs, behold, they laughed at them. And We did not show them any sign but it was greater than its fellow, and We seized them with punishment so that they might return.﴾ ﴿And they said, "O sorcerer, invoke your Lord for us by what He has covenanted with you. Indeed, we are guided."﴾ ﴿But when We removed the punishment from them, behold, they broke their word.﴾ ﴿And Pharaoh proclaimed among his people, saying, "O my people, is not the kingdom of Egypt mine, and these rivers flowing beneath me? Do you not see? Or am I better than this one who is contemptible and can hardly express himself? Why have bracelets of gold not been put upon him, or the angels not come with him in succession?"﴾ ﴿So he made his people feeble-minded, and they obeyed him. Indeed, they were a defiant people.﴾ ﴿And when they angered Us, We took vengeance upon them and drowned them all.﴾

In the verse there are several issues.

First issue: Know that the purpose of repeating the story of Moses, peace be upon him, and Pharaoh in this context is to confirm what was said earlier. This is because the disbelievers of Quraysh criticized the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ on the ground that he was poor, lacking wealth and status. So God Exalted explained that Moses, peace be upon him, after presenting the overpowering and dazzling miracles, about whose truth no sane person doubts, was met by Pharaoh with the same doubt that the disbelievers of Quraysh raised. He said: "I am rich, abounding in wealth and status. Do you not see that the kingdom of Egypt has come to me, and these rivers flow beneath me? As for Moses, he is poor and contemptible, and he has neither eloquence nor tongue. How can a poor man be a messenger from God to a great, wealthy king?" Thus it is established that this doubt which the disbelievers of Mecca raised, namely their saying ﴿Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a great man from the two cities?﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 31], was raised by Pharaoh against Moses in exactly the same words. Then We took vengeance upon them and drowned them. The purpose of mentioning this story is to confirm two matters:

One of them: that disbelievers and ignorant people always argue against the prophets with this feeble doubt, so it should be disregarded and not paid attention to.

The second: that Pharaoh, at the height of his worldly state, became humiliated and false, so the matter regarding your enemies will be likewise. Thus it is established that the purpose of repeating this story is not the very same story, but rather to confirm the answer to the aforementioned doubt. On this basis, this is not a retelling of the story at all. This is one of the finest investigations, and God knows best.

[Page 187]

Second issue, on interpreting the words: God mentioned that He sent Moses with His signs, namely the miracles that were with Moses, peace be upon him, to Pharaoh and his chiefs, that is, his people. Moses said, "I am a messenger of the Lord of the worlds." When he brought them those signs, behold, they laughed at them. It is said that when he cast down his staff and it became a serpent, then he took it and it returned to being a staff as it was, they laughed. And when he showed them the white hand, then it returned as it was, they laughed. If it is asked: how is it permissible to answer "lamma" (when) with "idha" (behold), which expresses sudden occurrence? We say: because the verb of sudden occurrence is implied with it; as if it were said: "When he brought them Our signs, they were suddenly at the time of their laughing."

* * *

Then He said: ﴿And We did not show them any sign but it was greater than its fellow.﴾ If it is asked: the apparent meaning of the words requires that each one be better than the one that follows, and that is impossible. We say: when the intention is to emphasize that each of those things reached the utmost degrees of excellence, this statement may be used in the sense that it is not unlikely, among people looking at them, that one says: "This is better than the second," and another says: "No, the second is better," and a third says: "No, the third is better." In that case each of those things is described as being better than the others.

* * *

Then God Exalted said: ﴿And We seized them with punishment so that they might return.﴾ That is, from disbelief to faith. The Mu'tazilites (a theological school) said: this indicates that He wills faith from all, and that He only manifested those overpowering miracles in order that they would return from disbelief to faith. The commentators said: the meaning of His words ﴿And We seized them with punishment﴾ is: with the things which He sent upon them, such as the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs, the blood, and the effacement.

* * *

Then God Exalted said: ﴿And they said, "O sorcerer, invoke your Lord for us by what He has covenanted with you. Indeed, we are guided."﴾ If it is asked: how did they call him a sorcerer while saying ﴿Indeed, we are guided﴾? We say: there are several aspects to this:

The first: they used to call a learned, skilled man a sorcerer, because they held magic in great esteem. Just as in our time it is said of a wondrous, accomplished worker that he has done magic.

The second: ﴿O sorcerer﴾ is according to the belief of the people and the common usage of Pharaoh's people, like His saying ﴿And they said, "O you to whom the Reminder has been sent down, indeed you are a madman!"﴾ [al-Hijr: 6]; that is, the Reminder was sent down upon him in their opinion and assumption.

The third: their saying ﴿Indeed, we are guided﴾ was made while they were resolved to the contrary. Do you not see His saying ﴿But when We removed the punishment from them, behold, they broke their word﴾? So their calling him a sorcerer does not contradict their saying ﴿Indeed, we are guided.﴾ Then God explained that when He removed the punishment from them, they broke that covenant.

When God Exalted related Pharaoh's treatment of Moses, He also related Pharaoh's treatment of his own people, saying: ﴿And Pharaoh proclaimed among his people﴾. The meaning is that he made this statement public, saying: ﴿O my people, is not the kingdom of Egypt mine, and these rivers flowing beneath me?﴾ meaning the rivers that they separated from the Nile. The greatest of them are four: the Royal River, the Tulun River, the Damietta River, and the Tinnis River. It is said that they flowed beneath his palace. The essence of the matter is that he argued, by the abundance of his wealth and the strength of his status, for his own superiority.

* * *

Then he said: ﴿Or am I better than this one who is contemptible and can hardly express himself?﴾ By his being contemptible he meant that he was poor and of weak condition, and by His saying ﴿can hardly express himself﴾ he meant a impediment that was in his tongue. They differed regarding the meaning of "am" (أمْ) here. Abu 'Ubayda said: its figurative sense is "rather" (بَلْ), and on this basis the speech is complete at His saying ﴿Do you not see?﴾, then he began: ﴿Or am I better than...﴾ in the sense of "rather, I am better." The others said: this "am" is connected, because the meaning is "Do you not see? Or do you see?" except that he placed his saying ﴿I am better﴾ in the place of "you see," because when they said to him, "You are better," they were, in his view, seers. Others said: the completion of the speech is at His saying "am," and His saying ﴿I am better﴾ is the beginning of the speech, and the implied meaning is: ﴿Do you not see?﴾ or do you see? But he suffices with mentioning "am," as you say to someone else: "Are you eating, am?" meaning: are you eating or are you not eating? You limit yourself to the word "am" out of preference for brevity. So it is here too.

If it is asked: did not Moses, peace be upon him, ask God to remove the impediment from his tongue, by his saying ﴿And loosen a knot from my tongue, that they may understand my speech﴾ [Ta-Ha: 27–28], and God granted him that by His saying ﴿You have been given your request, O Moses﴾ [Ta-Ha: 36]? Then how did Pharaoh reproach him with that impediment? The answer to this is in two aspects:

The first: Pharaoh by his saying ﴿and can hardly express himself﴾ meant his proof which indicates the truth of what he claims, and he did not mean that he had no ability to speak.

The second: he reproached him with what he had been formerly, for Moses had been with Pharaoh for a long time and had an impediment in his tongue. So Pharaoh attributed to him the impediment he had known him to have, because he did not know that God had removed that defect from him.

* * *

Then he said: ﴿Why have bracelets of gold not been put upon him?﴾ The intention is that the custom of the people was that when they made one of them their chief, they would put a golden bracelet on him and a golden collar around his neck. So Pharaoh demanded from Moses the like of this condition. The readers differed regarding "asawira" (أسْوِرَةٌ): some read "asawira" and others read "asawir" (أساوِرَةٌ). "Asawira" is the plural of "siwar" for small numbers, as you say "himar" and "ahmira," "ghurab" and "aghriba." As for the one who reads "asawir," it is because "asawir" is the plural of "aswar," which is the bracelet, and "asawir" has the "ha" as a replacement for the "ya," like "bitriq" and "batariqa," "zindiq" and "zanadiqa," "firzin" and "farazina." So "asawir" is the plural of "aswar." The essence of the discussion returns to one point, namely that Pharaoh used to say: "I have more wealth and status, so I must be better than him. Therefore it is impossible for him to be a messenger from God, because the station of prophethood requires that he be served, and the lowly cannot be served by the noble." Then the faulty premise is his saying: "Whoever has more wealth and status is better," and this is the very premise on which the disbelievers of Quraysh relied in their saying ﴿Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a great man from the two cities?﴾.

Then He said: ﴿Or the angels did not come with him in succession?﴾ It is possible that the meaning is "accompanying him," from your saying "I joined him to it, and so it was joined," and that it is from their saying "they joined together" in the sense of "they accompanied one another." Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is that they walk with him, and thereby they indicate the truth of his prophethood.

Then God Exalted said: ﴿So he made his people feeble-minded, and they obeyed him.﴾ That is, he asked them for lightness in carrying out what he commanded them, and they obeyed him. ﴿Indeed, they were a defiant people﴾, in that they obeyed that ignorant, defiant man. ﴿And when they angered Us﴾, that is, provoked Us. It is related that Ibn Jurayj became angry about something, and it was said to him: "Are you angry, O Abu Khalid?" He said: "The One who created forbearance has become angry. Indeed God says: ﴿And when they angered Us﴾", that is, provoked Us.

Then He, Exalted is He, said: "They did not present it to you except for disputation" (al-Zukhruf: 58), meaning: they did not present this example to you except for the sake of disputation and victory in speech, not seeking to distinguish truth from falsehood. "Rather, they are a contentious people" (al-Zukhruf: 58), exceeding in contention. This is because His saying, "Indeed, you and what you worship besides Allah" (al-Anbiya: 98), does not include the angels and Jesus. Its explanation is in several respects:

First: the word *ma* (what) does not at all include rational beings.

Second: the word *ma* is not explicit in universality, as evidenced by the fact that it is correct to add the words "all" and "some" to it, so one says: "Indeed, you and all that you worship besides Allah," or "Indeed, you and some of what you worship besides Allah."

Third: His saying, "Indeed, you and all that you worship besides Allah," or "and some of what you worship," is direct address, so perhaps there was no one among them who worshipped the Messiah or the angels.

Fourth: even granting that His saying, "Indeed, you and what you worship besides Allah," is general, the texts indicating the exaltation of the angels and Jesus are more specific than it, and the specific takes precedence over the general.

Fourth issue: Those who call for condemning disputation have held to this verse. However, we have mentioned in the explanation of His saying, "None dispute concerning the signs of Allah except those who disbelieve" (Ghafir: 4), that many verses indicate that disputation is praiseworthy and commendable. The way to reconcile is to direct those verses to disputation that establishes the truth, and to direct this verse to disputation that establishes falsehood.

"And had We willed" (al-Zukhruf: 60),

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We indeed sent Moses with Our signs to Pharaoh and his chiefs, and he said, "I am a messenger of the Lord of the worlds." But when he brought them Our signs, behold, they laughed at them. And We did not show them any sign but it was greater than its fellow, and We seized them with punishment so that they might return.﴾ ﴿And they said, "O sorcerer, invoke your Lord for us by what He has covenanted with you. Indeed, we are guided."﴾ ﴿But when We removed the punishment from them, behold, they broke their word.﴾ ﴿And Pharaoh proclaimed among his people, saying, "O my people, is not the kingdom of Egypt mine, and these rivers flowing beneath me? Do you not see? Or am I better than this one who is contemptible and can hardly express himself? Why have bracelets of gold not been put upon him, or the angels not come with him in succession?"﴾ ﴿So he made his people feeble-minded, and they obeyed him. Indeed, they were a defiant people.﴾ ﴿And when they angered Us, We took vengeance upon them and drowned them all.﴾

In the verse there are several issues.

First issue: Know that the purpose of repeating the story of Moses, peace be upon him, and Pharaoh in this context is to confirm what was said earlier. This is because the disbelievers of Quraysh criticized the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ on the ground that he was poor, lacking wealth and status. So God Exalted explained that Moses, peace be upon him, after presenting the overpowering and dazzling miracles, about whose truth no sane person doubts, was met by Pharaoh with the same doubt that the disbelievers of Quraysh raised. He said: "I am rich, abounding in wealth and status. Do you not see that the kingdom of Egypt has come to me, and these rivers flow beneath me? As for Moses, he is poor and contemptible, and he has neither eloquence nor tongue. How can a poor man be a messenger from God to a great, wealthy king?" Thus it is established that this doubt which the disbelievers of Mecca raised, namely their saying ﴿Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a great man from the two cities?﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 31], was raised by Pharaoh against Moses in exactly the same words. Then We took vengeance upon them and drowned them. The purpose of mentioning this story is to confirm two matters:

One of them: that disbelievers and ignorant people always argue against the prophets with this feeble doubt, so it should be disregarded and not paid attention to.

The second: that Pharaoh, at the height of his worldly state, became humiliated and false, so the matter regarding your enemies will be likewise. Thus it is established that the purpose of repeating this story is not the very same story, but rather to confirm the answer to the aforementioned doubt. On this basis, this is not a retelling of the story at all. This is one of the finest investigations, and God knows best.

[Page 187]

Second issue, on interpreting the words: God mentioned that He sent Moses with His signs, namely the miracles that were with Moses, peace be upon him, to Pharaoh and his chiefs, that is, his people. Moses said, "I am a messenger of the Lord of the worlds." When he brought them those signs, behold, they laughed at them. It is said that when he cast down his staff and it became a serpent, then he took it and it returned to being a staff as it was, they laughed. And when he showed them the white hand, then it returned as it was, they laughed. If it is asked: how is it permissible to answer "lamma" (when) with "idha" (behold), which expresses sudden occurrence? We say: because the verb of sudden occurrence is implied with it; as if it were said: "When he brought them Our signs, they were suddenly at the time of their laughing."

* * *

Then He said: ﴿And We did not show them any sign but it was greater than its fellow.﴾ If it is asked: the apparent meaning of the words requires that each one be better than the one that follows, and that is impossible. We say: when the intention is to emphasize that each of those things reached the utmost degrees of excellence, this statement may be used in the sense that it is not unlikely, among people looking at them, that one says: "This is better than the second," and another says: "No, the second is better," and a third says: "No, the third is better." In that case each of those things is described as being better than the others.

* * *

Then God Exalted said: ﴿And We seized them with punishment so that they might return.﴾ That is, from disbelief to faith. The Mu'tazilites (a theological school) said: this indicates that He wills faith from all, and that He only manifested those overpowering miracles in order that they would return from disbelief to faith. The commentators said: the meaning of His words ﴿And We seized them with punishment﴾ is: with the things which He sent upon them, such as the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs, the blood, and the effacement.

* * *

Then God Exalted said: ﴿And they said, "O sorcerer, invoke your Lord for us by what He has covenanted with you. Indeed, we are guided."﴾ If it is asked: how did they call him a sorcerer while saying ﴿Indeed, we are guided﴾? We say: there are several aspects to this:

The first: they used to call a learned, skilled man a sorcerer, because they held magic in great esteem. Just as in our time it is said of a wondrous, accomplished worker that he has done magic.

The second: ﴿O sorcerer﴾ is according to the belief of the people and the common usage of Pharaoh's people, like His saying ﴿And they said, "O you to whom the Reminder has been sent down, indeed you are a madman!"﴾ [al-Hijr: 6]; that is, the Reminder was sent down upon him in their opinion and assumption.

The third: their saying ﴿Indeed, we are guided﴾ was made while they were resolved to the contrary. Do you not see His saying ﴿But when We removed the punishment from them, behold, they broke their word﴾? So their calling him a sorcerer does not contradict their saying ﴿Indeed, we are guided.﴾ Then God explained that when He removed the punishment from them, they broke that covenant.

When God Exalted related Pharaoh's treatment of Moses, He also related Pharaoh's treatment of his own people, saying: ﴿And Pharaoh proclaimed among his people﴾. The meaning is that he made this statement public, saying: ﴿O my people, is not the kingdom of Egypt mine, and these rivers flowing beneath me?﴾ meaning the rivers that they separated from the Nile. The greatest of them are four: the Royal River, the Tulun River, the Damietta River, and the Tinnis River. It is said that they flowed beneath his palace. The essence of the matter is that he argued, by the abundance of his wealth and the strength of his status, for his own superiority.

* * *

Then he said: ﴿Or am I better than this one who is contemptible and can hardly express himself?﴾ By his being contemptible he meant that he was poor and of weak condition, and by His saying ﴿can hardly express himself﴾ he meant a impediment that was in his tongue. They differed regarding the meaning of "am" (أمْ) here. Abu 'Ubayda said: its figurative sense is "rather" (بَلْ), and on this basis the speech is complete at His saying ﴿Do you not see?﴾, then he began: ﴿Or am I better than...﴾ in the sense of "rather, I am better." The others said: this "am" is connected, because the meaning is "Do you not see? Or do you see?" except that he placed his saying ﴿I am better﴾ in the place of "you see," because when they said to him, "You are better," they were, in his view, seers. Others said: the completion of the speech is at His saying "am," and His saying ﴿I am better﴾ is the beginning of the speech, and the implied meaning is: ﴿Do you not see?﴾ or do you see? But he suffices with mentioning "am," as you say to someone else: "Are you eating, am?" meaning: are you eating or are you not eating? You limit yourself to the word "am" out of preference for brevity. So it is here too.

If it is asked: did not Moses, peace be upon him, ask God to remove the impediment from his tongue, by his saying ﴿And loosen a knot from my tongue, that they may understand my speech﴾ [Ta-Ha: 27–28], and God granted him that by His saying ﴿You have been given your request, O Moses﴾ [Ta-Ha: 36]? Then how did Pharaoh reproach him with that impediment? The answer to this is in two aspects:

The first: Pharaoh by his saying ﴿and can hardly express himself﴾ meant his proof which indicates the truth of what he claims, and he did not mean that he had no ability to speak.

The second: he reproached him with what he had been formerly, for Moses had been with Pharaoh for a long time and had an impediment in his tongue. So Pharaoh attributed to him the impediment he had known him to have, because he did not know that God had removed that defect from him.

* * *

Then he said: ﴿Why have bracelets of gold not been put upon him?﴾ The intention is that the custom of the people was that when they made one of them their chief, they would put a golden bracelet on him and a golden collar around his neck. So Pharaoh demanded from Moses the like of this condition. The readers differed regarding "asawira" (أسْوِرَةٌ): some read "asawira" and others read "asawir" (أساوِرَةٌ). "Asawira" is the plural of "siwar" for small numbers, as you say "himar" and "ahmira," "ghurab" and "aghriba." As for the one who reads "asawir," it is because "asawir" is the plural of "aswar," which is the bracelet, and "asawir" has the "ha" as a replacement for the "ya," like "bitriq" and "batariqa," "zindiq" and "zanadiqa," "firzin" and "farazina." So "asawir" is the plural of "aswar." The essence of the discussion returns to one point, namely that Pharaoh used to say: "I have more wealth and status, so I must be better than him. Therefore it is impossible for him to be a messenger from God, because the station of prophethood requires that he be served, and the lowly cannot be served by the noble." Then the faulty premise is his saying: "Whoever has more wealth and status is better," and this is the very premise on which the disbelievers of Quraysh relied in their saying ﴿Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a great man from the two cities?﴾.

Then He said: ﴿Or the angels did not come with him in succession?﴾ It is possible that the meaning is "accompanying him," from your saying "I joined him to it, and so it was joined," and that it is from their saying "they joined together" in the sense of "they accompanied one another." Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is that they walk with him, and thereby they indicate the truth of his prophethood.

* * *

Then God Exalted said: ﴿So he made his people feeble-minded, and they obeyed him.﴾ That is, he asked them for lightness in carrying out what he commanded them, and they obeyed him. ﴿Indeed, they were a defiant people﴾, in that they obeyed that ignorant, defiant man. ﴿And when they angered Us﴾, that is, provoked Us. It is related that Ibn Jurayj became angry about something, and it was said to him: "Are you angry, O Abu Khalid?" He said: "The One who created forbearance has become angry. Indeed God says: ﴿And when they angered Us﴾", that is, provoked Us.

Then God Exalted said: ﴿We took vengeance upon them﴾. Know that mention of the word "asaf" (anger/grief) with respect to God Exalted is impossible, and mention of the word "intiqam" (vengeance) and each of these two is among the ambiguous expressions which must be interpreted. The meaning of anger with respect to God is the will to punish, and the meaning of vengeance is the will to punish for a prior crime.

Then God Exalted said: ﴿So We made them a precedent and an example﴾. "Salaf" is everything you have sent ahead of you of righteous deeds or loans, so it is a "salaf." "Salaf" also refers to those among your fathers and relatives who have gone before, and its singular is "salif." From it is the saying of Tufayl, lamenting his people:

They passed on before, the path of their destination upon them, and the turning of death's events overturns men.

Accordingly, al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: He says: "We made them those who go before, so that others may take warning from them", that is, We made them a precedent for the disbelievers of the nation of Muhammad, peace be upon him. Al-Layth said: it is said "salufa," with a damma on the lam, "yaslufu," "sulufan," so he is "sulufun," that is, one who has gone before. His saying ﴿and an example for the later ones﴾ means: a lesson for those who remain after them, and a sign and a lesson. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: "mathal" (example) is singular but is intended as plural, and for this reason it is conjoined with "salaf." And God knows best.

In the verse there are several issues.

First issue: Know that He Exalted mentioned many kinds of their disbelieving statements in this surah, and answered them with many aspects:

The first of them: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they have made for Him from His servants a portion﴾.

The second of them: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they have made the angels, who are the servants of the Most Merciful, females﴾.

The third of them: His saying: ﴿And they said, "Had the Most Merciful willed, we would not have worshipped them"﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 20].

Fourth: His saying, "And they say, 'Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a man from the two cities, a great one?'" (al-Zukhruf: 31).

Fifth: This is the verse we are now explaining. The wording of the verse indicates only that when the son of Mary was presented as an example, the people began to clamor and raise their voices. As for what that example was like and in what respect it was, the wording does not indicate it. The exegetes have mentioned several explanations for it, all of which are possible:

The first: When the disbelievers heard that the Christians worship Jesus, they said, "If they worship Jesus, then our gods are better than Jesus." They only said this because they were worshipping the angels.

The second: It is narrated that when His saying, Exalted is He, "Indeed, you and what you worship besides Allah are the fuel of Hell" (al-Anbiya: 98) was revealed, Abdullah ibn al-Zib'ara said, "Is this specific to us and our gods, or is it for all nations?" The Prophet ﷺ said, "Rather, it is for all nations." He said, "I have defeated you, by the Lord of the Ka'bah! Do you not claim that Jesus son of Mary is a prophet, and you praise him and his mother with goodness? I know that the Christians worship them both, and the Jews worship Uzayr, and the angels are worshipped. If these are in the Fire, then we are content that we and our gods be with them." The Prophet ﷺ fell silent, the people rejoiced, laughed and clamored. Then Allah, Exalted is He, revealed: "Indeed, those for whom the good has preceded from Us, those are kept far away from it" (al-Anbiya: 101). This verse was also revealed. The meaning: When Abdullah ibn al-Zib'ara presented Jesus "the son of Mary as an example" and disputed with the Messenger of Allah regarding the worship of the Christians of him,

"behold, your people" — Quraysh — "from it" — that is, from this example — "turn away" — that is, a clamor and uproar rises up from them in joy, disputation and laughter because of what they saw of the silencing of the Messenger of Allah. It is customary that when one of two opponents is silenced, the other opponent shows joy and clamor. "And they said, 'Are our gods better, or is he?'" meaning: our gods in your view are not better than Jesus, so if Jesus is among the fuel of Hell, the matter of our gods is even less.

The third explanation: When the Prophet ﷺ related that the Christians worshipped the Messiah and made him a god for themselves, the disbelievers of Makkah said, "Muhammad wants to make for us a god just as the Christians made the Messiah a god for themselves." Then, at this point, they said, "Are our gods better, or is he?" meaning: are our gods better, or Muhammad? They mentioned this because they said, "Muhammad calls us to worship himself, and our fathers claimed that it is obligatory to worship these idols. If one of these two matters is unavoidable, then worshipping these idols is preferable, because our fathers and forefathers agreed upon it, whereas Muhammad is accused in our affair of seeking to be worshipped." So occupation with worshipping idols was preferable. Then He, Exalted is He, clarified that we did not say that occupation with worshipping the Messiah is a good path; rather, it is false speech, for Jesus is nothing but a servant upon whom We bestowed favour. If the matter is so, then their doubt in their saying that Muhammad wants to command us to worship himself has been removed. These three explanations are such that each of them is possible in the wording of the verse.

Moses said, "I am a messenger of the Lord of the worlds." When he brought them those signs, behold, they laughed at them. It is said that when he cast down his staff and it became a serpent, then he took it and it returned to being a staff as it was, they laughed. And when he showed them the white hand, then it returned as it was, they laughed. If it is asked: how is it permissible to answer "lamma" (when) with "idha" (behold), which expresses sudden occurrence? We say: because the verb of sudden occurrence is implied with it; as if it were said: "When he brought them Our signs, they were suddenly at the time of their laughing."

* * *

Then He said: ﴿And We did not show them any sign but it was greater than its fellow.﴾ If it is asked: the apparent meaning of the words requires that each one be better than the one that follows, and that is impossible. We say: when the intention is to emphasize that each of those things reached the utmost degrees of excellence, this statement may be used in the sense that it is not unlikely, among people looking at them, that one says: "This is better than the second," and another says: "No, the second is better," and a third says: "No, the third is better." In that case each of those things is described as being better than the others.

* * *

Then God Exalted said: ﴿And We seized them with punishment so that they might return.﴾ That is, from disbelief to faith. The Mu'tazilites (a theological school) said: this indicates that He wills faith from all, and that He only manifested those overpowering miracles in order that they would return from disbelief to faith. The commentators said: the meaning of His words ﴿And We seized them with punishment﴾ is: with the things which He sent upon them, such as the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs, the blood, and the effacement.

* * *

Then God Exalted said: ﴿And they said, "O sorcerer, invoke your Lord for us by what He has covenanted with you. Indeed, we are guided."﴾ If it is asked: how did they call him a sorcerer while saying ﴿Indeed, we are guided﴾? We say: there are several aspects to this:

The first: they used to call a learned, skilled man a sorcerer, because they held magic in great esteem. Just as in our time it is said of a wondrous, accomplished worker that he has done magic.

The second: ﴿O sorcerer﴾ is according to the belief of the people and the common usage of Pharaoh's people, like His saying ﴿And they said, "O you to whom the Reminder has been sent down, indeed you are a madman!"﴾ [al-Hijr: 6]; that is, the Reminder was sent down upon him in their opinion and assumption.

The third: their saying ﴿Indeed, we are guided﴾ was made while they were resolved to the contrary. Do you not see His saying ﴿But when We removed the punishment from them, behold, they broke their word﴾? So their calling him a sorcerer does not contradict their saying ﴿Indeed, we are guided.﴾ Then God explained that when He removed the punishment from them, they broke that covenant.

When God Exalted related Pharaoh's treatment of Moses, He also related Pharaoh's treatment of his own people, saying: ﴿And Pharaoh proclaimed among his people﴾. The meaning is that he made this statement public, saying: ﴿O my people, is not the kingdom of Egypt mine, and these rivers flowing beneath me?﴾ meaning the rivers that they separated from the Nile. The greatest of them are four: the Royal River, the Tulun River, the Damietta River, and the Tinnis River. It is said that they flowed beneath his palace. The essence of the matter is that he argued, by the abundance of his wealth and the strength of his status, for his own superiority.

* * *

Then he said: ﴿Or am I better than this one who is contemptible and can hardly express himself?﴾ By his being contemptible he meant that he was poor and of weak condition, and by His saying ﴿can hardly express himself﴾ he meant a impediment that was in his tongue. They differed regarding the meaning of "am" (أمْ) here. Abu 'Ubayda said: its figurative sense is "rather" (بَلْ), and on this basis the speech is complete at His saying ﴿Do you not see?﴾, then he began: ﴿Or am I better than...﴾ in the sense of "rather, I am better." The others said: this "am" is connected, because the meaning is "Do you not see? Or do you see?" except that he placed his saying ﴿I am better﴾ in the place of "you see," because when they said to him, "You are better," they were, in his view, seers. Others said: the completion of the speech is at His saying "am," and His saying ﴿I am better﴾ is the beginning of the speech, and the implied meaning is: ﴿Do you not see?﴾ or do you see? But he suffices with mentioning "am," as you say to someone else: "Are you eating, am?" meaning: are you eating or are you not eating? You limit yourself to the word "am" out of preference for brevity. So it is here too.

If it is asked: did not Moses, peace be upon him, ask God to remove the impediment from his tongue, by his saying ﴿And loosen a knot from my tongue, that they may understand my speech﴾ [Ta-Ha: 27–28], and God granted him that by His saying ﴿You have been given your request, O Moses﴾ [Ta-Ha: 36]? Then how did Pharaoh reproach him with that impediment? The answer to this is in two aspects:

The first: Pharaoh by his saying ﴿and can hardly express himself﴾ meant his proof which indicates the truth of what he claims, and he did not mean that he had no ability to speak.

The second: he reproached him with what he had been formerly, for Moses had been with Pharaoh for a long time and had an impediment in his tongue. So Pharaoh attributed to him the impediment he had known him to have, because he did not know that God had removed that defect from him.

* * *

Then he said: ﴿Why have bracelets of gold not been put upon him?﴾ The intention is that the custom of the people was that when they made one of them their chief, they would put a golden bracelet on him and a golden collar around his neck. So Pharaoh demanded from Moses the like of this condition. The readers differed regarding "asawira" (أسْوِرَةٌ): some read "asawira" and others read "asawir" (أساوِرَةٌ). "Asawira" is the plural of "siwar" for small numbers, as you say "himar" and "ahmira," "ghurab" and "aghriba." As for the one who reads "asawir," it is because "asawir" is the plural of "aswar," which is the bracelet, and "asawir" has the "ha" as a replacement for the "ya," like "bitriq" and "batariqa," "zindiq" and "zanadiqa," "firzin" and "farazina." So "asawir" is the plural of "aswar." The essence of the discussion returns to one point, namely that Pharaoh used to say: "I have more wealth and status, so I must be better than him. Therefore it is impossible for him to be a messenger from God, because the station of prophethood requires that he be served, and the lowly cannot be served by the noble." Then the faulty premise is his saying: "Whoever has more wealth and status is better," and this is the very premise on which the disbelievers of Quraysh relied in their saying ﴿Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a great man from the two cities?﴾.

Then He said: ﴿Or the angels did not come with him in succession?﴾ It is possible that the meaning is "accompanying him," from your saying "I joined him to it, and so it was joined," and that it is from their saying "they joined together" in the sense of "they accompanied one another." Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is that they walk with him, and thereby they indicate the truth of his prophethood.

* * *

Then God Exalted said: ﴿So he made his people feeble-minded, and they obeyed him.﴾ That is, he asked them for lightness in carrying out what he commanded them, and they obeyed him. ﴿Indeed, they were a defiant people﴾, in that they obeyed that ignorant, defiant man. ﴿And when they angered Us﴾, that is, provoked Us. It is related that Ibn Jurayj became angry about something, and it was said to him: "Are you angry, O Abu Khalid?" He said: "The One who created forbearance has become angry. Indeed God says: ﴿And when they angered Us﴾", that is, provoked Us.

* * *

Then God Exalted said: ﴿We took vengeance upon them﴾. Know that mention of the word "asaf" (anger/grief) with respect to God Exalted is impossible, and mention of the word "intiqam" (vengeance) and each of these two is among the ambiguous expressions which must be interpreted. The meaning of anger with respect to God is the will to punish, and the meaning of vengeance is the will to punish for a prior crime.

* * *

Then God Exalted said: ﴿So We made them a precedent and an example﴾. "Salaf" is everything you have sent ahead of you of righteous deeds or loans, so it is a "salaf." "Salaf" also refers to those among your fathers and relatives who have gone before, and its singular is "salif." From it is the saying of Tufayl, lamenting his people:

They passed on before, the path of their destination upon them, and the turning of death's events overturns men.

Accordingly, al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: He says: "We made them those who go before, so that others may take warning from them", that is, We made them a precedent for the disbelievers of the nation of Muhammad, peace be upon him. Most of the readers read it with a fatha ("salafan"), and it is the plural of "salif" as we have mentioned. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "sulafan" (سُلَفًا) with a damma, which is the plural of "salaf." Al-Layth said: it is said "salufa," with a damma on the lam, "yaslufu," "sulufan," so he is "sulufun," that is, one who has gone before. His saying ﴿and an example for the later ones﴾ means: a lesson for those who remain after them, and a sign and a lesson. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: "mathal" (example) is singular but is intended as plural, and for this reason it is conjoined with "salaf." The proof that it applies to more than one is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿God sets forth an example: a servant owned, who has power over nothing, and one whom We have given goodly provision from Us﴾ [al-Nahl: 75], where He placed two things under "example." And God knows best.

* *

[Page 189]

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And when the son of Mary is cited as an example, behold, your people turn away from it. And they said, "Are our gods better, or is he?" They only cited it to you for argument. Indeed, they are a contentious people. He is only a servant upon whom We bestowed favor, and We made him an example for the Children of Israel. And if We willed, We would have made from among you angels to succeed on the earth. And indeed, he is a sign for the Hour, so do not be in doubt about it, and follow Me. This is a straight path. And let not Satan avert you; indeed, he is to you a clear enemy.﴾ 50

In the verse there are several issues.

First issue: Know that He Exalted mentioned many kinds of their disbelieving statements in this surah, and answered them with many aspects:

The first of them: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they have made for Him from His servants a portion﴾.

The second of them: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they have made the angels, who are the servants of the Most Merciful, females﴾.

The third of them: His saying: ﴿And they said, "Had the Most Merciful willed, we would not have worshipped them"﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 20].

Fourth: His saying, "And they say, 'Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a man from the two cities, a great one?'" (al-Zukhruf: 31).

Fifth: This is the verse we are now explaining. The wording of the verse indicates only that when the son of Mary was presented as an example, the people began to clamor and raise their voices. As for what that example was like and in what respect it was, the wording does not indicate it. The exegetes have mentioned several explanations for it, all of which are possible:

The first: When the disbelievers heard that the Christians worship Jesus, they said, "If they worship Jesus, then our gods are better than Jesus." They only said this because they were worshipping the angels.

The second: It is narrated that when His saying, Exalted is He, "Indeed, you and what you worship besides Allah are the fuel of Hell" (al-Anbiya: 98) was revealed, Abdullah ibn al-Zib'ara said, "Is this specific to us and our gods, or is it for all nations?" The Prophet ﷺ said, "Rather, it is for all nations." He said, "I have defeated you, by the Lord of the Ka'bah! Do you not claim that Jesus son of Mary is a prophet, and you praise him and his mother with goodness? I know that the Christians worship them both, and the Jews worship Uzayr, and the angels are worshipped. If these are in the Fire, then we are content that we and our gods be with them." The Prophet ﷺ fell silent, the people rejoiced, laughed and clamored. Then Allah, Exalted is He, revealed: "Indeed, those for whom the good has preceded from Us, those are kept far away from it" (al-Anbiya: 101). This verse was also revealed. The meaning: When Abdullah ibn al-Zib'ara presented Jesus "the son of Mary as an example" and disputed with the Messenger of Allah regarding the worship of the Christians of him,
page 190
"behold, your people" — Quraysh — "from it" — that is, from this example — "turn away" — that is, a clamor and uproar rises up from them in joy, disputation and laughter because of what they saw of the silencing of the Messenger of Allah. It is customary that when one of two opponents is silenced, the other opponent shows joy and clamor. "And they said, 'Are our gods better, or is he?'" meaning: our gods in your view are not better than Jesus, so if Jesus is among the fuel of Hell, the matter of our gods is even less.

The third explanation: When the Prophet ﷺ related that the Christians worshipped the Messiah and made him a god for themselves, the disbelievers of Makkah said, "Muhammad wants to make for us a god just as the Christians made the Messiah a god for themselves." Then, at this point, they said, "Are our gods better, or is he?" meaning: are our gods better, or Muhammad? They mentioned this because they said, "Muhammad calls us to worship himself, and our fathers claimed that it is obligatory to worship these idols. If one of these two matters is unavoidable, then worshipping these idols is preferable, because our fathers and forefathers agreed upon it, whereas Muhammad is accused in our affair of seeking to be worshipped." So occupation with worshipping idols was preferable. Then He, Exalted is He, clarified that we did not say that occupation with worshipping the Messiah is a good path; rather, it is false speech, for Jesus is nothing but a servant upon whom We bestowed favour. If the matter is so, then their doubt in their saying that Muhammad wants to command us to worship himself has been removed. These three explanations are such that each of them is possible in the wording of the verse.

Second issue: Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, al-Kisa'i and Abu Bakr from 'Asim read "yasuddun" with a dammah on the sad, which is the reading of 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, peace be upon him. The rest read it with a kasrah on the sad, which is the reading of Ibn 'Abbas. They differed: al-Kisa'i said, "They have the same meaning, like ya'rishun and ya'rushun, and ya'kifun and ya'kufun." Among them some distinguished: As for the reading with a dammah, it is from *al-sudud* (turning away), meaning because of this example they turn away from the truth and avoid it; as for the reading with a kasrah, its meaning is clamoring.

Third issue: 'Asim, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "a-alihatuna" as an interrogative with two hamzahs, the second being prolonged; the rest read it as an interrogative with one hamzah and a madd.

* * *

Then He, Exalted is He, said: "They did not present it to you except for disputation" (al-Zukhruf: 58), meaning: they did not present this example to you except for the sake of disputation and victory in speech, not seeking to distinguish truth from falsehood. "Rather, they are a contentious people" (al-Zukhruf: 58), exceeding in contention. This is because His saying, "Indeed, you and what you worship besides Allah" (al-Anbiya: 98), does not include the angels and Jesus. Its explanation is in several respects:

First: the word *ma* (what) does not at all include rational beings.

Second: the word *ma* is not explicit in universality, as evidenced by the fact that it is correct to add the words "all" and "some" to it, so one says: "Indeed, you and all that you worship besides Allah," or "Indeed, you and some of what you worship besides Allah."

Third: His saying, "Indeed, you and all that you worship besides Allah," or "and some of what you worship," is direct address, so perhaps there was no one among them who worshipped the Messiah or the angels.

Fourth: even granting that His saying, "Indeed, you and what you worship besides Allah," is general, the texts indicating the exaltation of the angels and Jesus are more specific than it, and the specific takes precedence over the general.

Fourth issue: Those who call for condemning disputation have held to this verse. However, we have mentioned in the explanation of His saying, "None dispute concerning the signs of Allah except those who disbelieve" (Ghafir: 4), that many verses indicate that disputation is praiseworthy and commendable. The way to reconcile is to direct those verses to disputation that establishes the truth, and to direct this verse to disputation that establishes falsehood.

* * *

Then He, Exalted is He, said: "He is only a servant upon whom We bestowed favour" (al-Zukhruf: 59), meaning: Jesus is nothing but a servant like other servants, upon whom We bestowed favour by making him a sign, creating him without a father as We created Adam, honouring him with prophethood, and making him a wondrous lesson, like a well-known proverb. "And had We willed" (al-Zukhruf: 60),
page 191
"We would have made from among you" — We would have produced from you, O men — "angels upon the earth succeeding" (al-Zukhruf: 60), as your children succeed you; just as We produced Jesus from a female without a male, so that you may know Our distinction by the overwhelming power, and so that you may know that the occurrence of begetting and being begotten among angels is a possible matter, while the Essence of Allah is exalted above that. "And indeed, he" — that is, Jesus — "is a sign of the Hour" (al-Zukhruf: 61), a condition of its portents by which it is known. The condition that indicates a thing is called a knowledge, because knowledge of it is obtained through it. Ibn 'Abbas read "la-'alamun," which means a sign. It was also read "lil-'ilm," and Ubayy read "la-dhikr." In a hadith: "Jesus will descend at a mountain pass in the holy land called Afiq, with a spear in his hand, and with it he will kill the Dajjal. He will come to Bayt al-Maqdis at the dawn prayer while the imam is leading them; the imam will draw back, and Jesus will move him forward and pray behind him according to the law of Muhammad ﷺ. Then he will kill the swine, break the cross, destroy the churches and synagogues, and kill the Christians except those who believe in him." "So do not be in doubt about it" (al-Zukhruf: 61), from *al-mirya*, which is doubt. "And follow Me" (al-Zukhruf: 61), follow My guidance and My law. "This is a straight path" (al-Zukhruf: 61), meaning: this to which I call you is a straight path. "And let not Satan avert you; indeed, he is to you a clear enemy" (al-Zukhruf: 62), whose enmity has become evident to you, because he is the one who expelled your father from the Garden and stripped from him the garment of light.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 43, verses 63–66:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when Jesus came with clear proofs, he said, "I have certainly come to you with wisdom, and to make clear to you some of that about which you differ. So fear Allah and obey me. Indeed, Allah is my Lord and your Lord, so worship Him; this is a straight path."﴾ ﴿But the factions differed among themselves; so woe to those who wronged, from the punishment of a painful day.﴾ ﴿Do they await except the Hour, that it will come upon them suddenly while they do not perceive?﴾

Know that He, exalted is He, mentioned that when Jesus came with the miracles and the clear, evident laws, ﴿he said, "I have certainly come to you with wisdom"﴾, and it is the knowledge of the Essence of Allah, His attributes and His acts. ﴿"And to make clear to you some of that about which you differ"﴾ meaning that the people of Moses had differed about matters of the legal obligations (ahkam al-taklif) and agreed upon other matters, so Jesus came to make the truth clear to them concerning those disputed issues. In summary: wisdom means the foundations of the religion (usul al-din), and "some of that about which they differ" means the branches of the religion (furu al-din). If it is said: why did he not make clear to them all that about which they differ? We say: because people may differ about things they have no need to know, so it is not obligatory upon the Messenger to clarify them. When he had made clear the foundations and the branches, he said: ﴿"So fear Allah"﴾ by disbelieving in Him and turning away from His religion, ﴿"and obey me"﴾ in what I convey to you of the obligations. ﴿"Indeed, Allah is my Lord and your Lord, so worship Him; this is a straight path"﴾, and its meaning is clear. ﴿But the factions differed﴾, that is, the sects that formed parties after Jesus, namely the Melkites, the Jacobites and the Nestorians; it was also said: the Jews and the Christians. ﴿So woe to those who wronged, from the punishment of a painful day﴾, and this is a warning of the Day of the Factions. If it is said: regarding His saying ﴿from among them﴾, to whom does the pronoun refer? We say: to those whom Jesus addressed in His saying ﴿"I have certainly come to you with wisdom"﴾, and they are his people.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿Do they await except the Hour, that it will come upon them suddenly?﴾ His saying "that it will come upon them" is a substitute (badal) for "the Hour," and the meaning is: do they await except the coming of the Hour? If they say: His saying "suddenly" conveys the very same meaning as His saying "while they do not perceive," so what is the benefit of it? We say: it is possible that it comes upon them suddenly while they know of it because they witness it.

The second of the judgments of the Day of Resurrection: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O My servants, no fear shall be upon you this Day, nor shall you grieve﴾. We have mentioned several times that the custom of the Qur'an is to restrict the term "servants" (ʿibad) to the believing, obedient, and God-fearing. His saying "O My servants" is the speech of God, exalted is He, as if the Truth Himself addresses them and says to them: ﴿O My servants, no fear shall be upon you this Day, nor shall you grieve﴾. In it are many kinds of things that necessitate joy:

The first: that the Truth, glorified and exalted is He, addressed them Himself without an intermediary.

The second: that He, exalted is He, described them with servanthood ('ubudiyyah), and this is a great honor, as evidenced by the fact that when He wished to honor Muhammad ﷺ on the night of the Ascension He said: ﴿Glory be to Him who took His servant by night﴾ [al-Isra'; 1].

The third: His saying ﴿no fear shall be upon you this Day﴾, whereby He removed fear from them entirely on the Day of Resurrection, and this is among the greatest of blessings.

The fourth: His saying ﴿nor shall you grieve﴾, whereby He negated from them grief over the loss of the past world.

* * *
Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Those who believed in Our signs and were Muslims﴾. It has been said: ﴿Those who believed﴾ is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is implied, the sense being: it will be said to them, "Enter Paradise." It is also possible that the meaning is: "I mean those who believed."

Muqatil said: when fear occurs on the Day of Resurrection, a caller will call out: ﴿O My servants, no fear shall be upon you this Day﴾; when they hear the call, the creatures raise their heads, and it is said: ﴿Those who believed in Our signs and were Muslims﴾, whereupon the people of false religions lower their heads.

The third judgment of the events of the Resurrection: when He, exalted is He, grants security to the believers from fear and grief, their reckoning must pass in the easiest and best manner; then it is said to them: ﴿Enter Paradise, you and your spouses, delighted﴾. The word "habrah" (delight) means extreme honor in what is described as beautiful; that is, they are honored with honor in the manner of exaggeration. This has already been explained in Surat al-Rum.

* * *
Then He said: ﴿Vessels of gold and cups will be circulated among them﴾. Al-Farra' said: the kub is a cup with a rounded head and no handle. So His saying ﴿vessels of gold﴾ is an indication of food, and His saying ﴿and cups﴾ is an indication of drink. Then He, exalted is He, left out detail and mentioned a general statement, saying: ﴿and therein is whatever the souls desire and the eyes delight in, and you therein will abide eternally﴾.
* * *
Then He said: ﴿And that is Paradise, which you have been given as an inheritance for what you used to do﴾. We have mentioned two views regarding the inheritance of Paradise in His saying: ﴿Those are the inheritors, who will inherit Paradise-Firdaws﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 10, 11]. And since He mentioned food and drink earlier, He here mentions the state of fruit, saying: ﴿For you therein is abundant fruit, from which you will eat﴾.
Know that He, exalted is He, sent Muhammad ﷺ first to the Arabs, then secondly to all the worlds. The Arabs were in severe hardship because of food, drink, and fruit; for this reason God, exalted is He, bestowed upon them these meanings again and again, in order to complete their desire and strengthen their motives.
