So His saying ﴿vessels of gold﴾ is an indication of food, and His saying ﴿and cups﴾ is an indication of drink. Then He, exalted is He, left out detail and mentioned a general statement, saying: ﴿and therein is whatever the souls desire and the eyes delight in, and you therein will abide eternally﴾.
* * *
Then He said: ﴿And that is Paradise, which you have been given as an inheritance for what you used to do﴾. We have mentioned two views regarding the inheritance of Paradise in His saying: ﴿Those are the inheritors, who will inherit Paradise-Firdaws﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 10, 11]. And since He mentioned food and drink earlier, He here mentions the state of fruit, saying: ﴿For you therein is abundant fruit, from which you will eat﴾.
Know that He, exalted is He, sent Muhammad ﷺ first to the Arabs, then secondly to all the worlds. The Arabs were in severe hardship because of food, drink, and fruit; for this reason God, exalted is He, bestowed upon them these meanings again and again, in order to complete their desire and strengthen their motives.

[Page 194]

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, the criminals will abide in the punishment of Hell.﴾ ﴿It will not be lightened for them, and they will be in it in despair.﴾ ﴿We did not wrong them, but they were the wrongdoers.﴾ ﴿And they will call, "O Malik, let your Lord put an end to us." He will say, "Indeed, you will remain."﴾ ﴿We have certainly brought you the truth, but most of you are averse to the truth.﴾ ﴿Or have they decided on a matter? Then indeed, We decide.﴾ ﴿Or do they think that We do not hear their secret and their private conversation? Yes, and Our messengers are with them, recording.﴾

Know that when Allah mentioned the promise, He followed it with the threat, in the continuous order found in the Qur'an. In this passage there are several issues.

The first issue: al-Qadi (the judge, i.e. ʿAbd al-Jabbar, the Muʿtazilite theologian) argued for the definite承 of the threat against sinners by His saying: ﴿Indeed, the criminals will abide in the punishment of Hell.﴾ ﴿It will not be lightened for them, and they will be in it in despair.﴾ The word "criminal" (mujrim) includes the disbeliever and the grave sinner, so it is necessary that all of them are in the punishment of Hell. His saying "abide" indicates eternity, and His saying "it will not be lightened for them" also indicates eternity and perpetuity.

The answer: what precedes this verse and what follows it indicates that the intended meaning of "criminals" here is the disbelievers. As for what precedes this verse, He said: ﴿O My servants, no fear will be upon you today, nor will you grieve,﴾ ﴿those who believed in Our verses and were Muslims.﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 68–69]. This indicates that everyone who believed in the signs of Allah and was Muslim will enter under His saying: ﴿O My servants, no fear will be upon you today, nor will you grieve, those who believed in Our verses and were Muslims.﴾ The grave sinner among the people of prayer believed in Allah the Exalted, His signs, and submitted, so it is necessary that he is included in that promise, and it is necessary that he is excluded from this threat. As for what follows this verse, it is His saying: ﴿We have certainly brought you the truth, but most of you are averse to the truth.﴾ The "truth" here means either Islam or the Qur'an, and a Muslim man does not dislike Islam or the Qur'an. Thus it is established that what precedes this verse and what follows it indicates that the intended meaning of "criminals" is the disbelievers. And Allah knows best.

The second issue: He the Exalted described the punishment of Hell, regarding the criminals, with three attributes.

The first: "abiding" (khulud). We have mentioned in many places that it is an expression for a long duration of stay, and it does not necessarily indicate perpetuity.

The second: His saying ﴿It will not be lightened for them﴾, meaning it will not be reduced or diminished. It comes from their saying: "The fever abated from him" (faturat ʿanhu al-humma) when it subsided and its heat decreased.

The third: His saying ﴿and they will be in it in despair﴾. The mubli s (one in despair) is the one who is silent with the silence of one who has despaired of relief. From al-Dahhak: the criminal will be placed in a coffin of fire, then it will be closed upon him, and he will remain in it, abiding, unseen. The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari, the Kashshaf) said: it has been read as (wa-hum fīhā), meaning: and they are in the Fire.

The third issue: al-Qadi argued with His saying: ﴿We did not wrong them, but they were the wrongdoers.﴾ He said: If He created disbelief in them in order to make them enter the Fire, then what is it that He negated by His saying "We did not wrong them"? And what is it that He attributed to them of what He negated from Himself? Would not affirming it as injustice to them be no more than what the people say? If they say: that act did not occur by the power of Allah the Mighty and Majestic alone, but occurred by the power of Allah together with the power of the servant jointly, then it was not an injustice from Allah.

We say: According to you, the power to do injustice necessitates injustice, and the Creator of that power is Allah the Exalted. So it is as if He, the Exalted, when He created in them the power to disbelieve along with creating disbelief, went out of being unjust to them, and that is impossible, because whoever is unjust in an act, when he does with it what necessitates that act, is more deserving of that description. So it is said to al-Qadi: Is the power of the servant suitable for both alternatives, or is it determined for one of the two alternatives? If it is suitable for both alternatives, then if the preference occurs without a preferring cause, the existence of the Creator is necessitated to be denied; and if it requires a preferring cause, the first division returns regarding it, and it must end in a preferring motive which Allah creates in the servant. And if it is determined for one of the two alternatives, then at that point what you have raised against us is binding upon you.

[Page 195]

Know that the man is not one who sees the line of argument and mentions it; rather, the man is one who looks at what precedes the statement and what follows it. If he sees it as coming upon his own school of thought exactly, he does not mention it. And Allah knows best.

The fourth issue: Ibn Masʿud read (yā Mālu) by dropping the kāf for the sake of apocope (tarkhīm). It was said to Ibn ʿAbbas: Ibn Masʿud read: "And they will call, O Mālu." He said: How preoccupied the people of the Fire are from this apocope! It was answered that this apocope was only fitting because it indicates that they had reached such weakness and emaciation that they could not utter from the word except part of it.

The fifth issue: They differed about the manner in which they made their request in His saying: ﴿O Malik, let your Lord put an end to us.﴾ Some of them said: it is by way of wishing. Others said: it is by way of seeking help, since they know that there is no escape for them from that punishment. It was also said: it is not far-fetched to say that because of the severity of what they are in of punishment, they forgot that request and so mentioned it by way of asking. Then He the Exalted explained that Malik says to them: ﴿Indeed, you will remain.﴾ The Qur'an does not say when he answered them: did he answer them immediately, or after a long period? And if it was after that, did that answer come a short time after that request, or a long time? There is nothing to prevent that the answer be delayed, as a way of belittling them and increasing their distress. It is reported from ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿUmar that it was after forty years, from others after a hundred years, and from Ibn ʿAbbas after a thousand years. And Allah knows best the exact measure of that.

Then He the Exalted explained that when Malik answered them with His saying ﴿Indeed, you will remain,﴾ He mentioned after it what is like the reason for that answer, saying: ﴿We have certainly brought you the truth, but most of you are averse to the truth.﴾ What is meant is their aversion toward Muhammad and the Qur'an, and the intensity of their hatred for accepting the true religion. If it is said: How does He say ﴿and they will call, O Malik﴾ after describing them with despair? We say: those are long periods and extended ages, so their conditions vary, and they fall silent at times due to the overwhelming of despair upon them, and they cry for help at times because of the severity of what they suffer. It is narrated that hunger will be inflicted upon the people of the Fire until it balances the punishment they are in, so they say: Call upon Malik, and they call: ﴿And they will call, O Malik, let your Lord put an end to us.﴾

When Allah the Exalted mentioned the manner of their punishment in the Hereafter, He then mentioned the manner of their deceit and the corruption of their inner state in this world, saying: ﴿Or have they decided on a matter? Then indeed, We decide.﴾ The meaning: "Or have they decided" — that is, the polytheists of Mecca have decided upon a matter of their plotting and scheming against the Messenger of Allah — "then indeed, We decide Our plan, just as they decided their plan." Like His saying: ﴿Or do they intend a plot? But those who disbelieved, they are the ones plotted against.﴾ [at-Tur: 42]. Muqatil said: it was revealed concerning their planning to scheme against him in the Dar al-Nadwa (the assembly house of Quraysh), and that is what Allah mentioned in His saying: ﴿And when those who disbelieved plotted against you﴾ [al-Anfal: 30]. We have mentioned the story.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿Or do they think that We do not hear their secret and their private conversation?﴾ The secret (sirr) is what a man speaks to himself or to another in a private place, and the private conversation (najwa) is what they speak among themselves. ﴿Yes,﴾ We hear it and are aware of it. ﴿And Our messengers﴾ — he means the guardian angels — ﴿are recording﴾ those states against them. It is reported from Yahya ibn Muʿadh: Whoever conceals his sins from people, and displays them to One from whom nothing in the heavens is hidden, has made Him the least of those who look at him, and this is one of the signs of hypocrisy.

His saying "abide" indicates eternity, and His saying "it will not be lightened for them" also indicates eternity and perpetuity.

The answer: what precedes this verse and what follows it indicates that the intended meaning of "criminals" here is the disbelievers. As for what precedes this verse, He said: ﴿O My servants, no fear will be upon you today, nor will you grieve,﴾ ﴿those who believed in Our verses and were Muslims.﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 68–69]. This indicates that everyone who believed in the signs of Allah and was Muslim will enter under His saying: ﴿O My servants, no fear will be upon you today, nor will you grieve, those who believed in Our verses and were Muslims.﴾ The grave sinner among the people of prayer believed in Allah the Exalted, His signs, and submitted, so it is necessary that he is included in that promise, and it is necessary that he is excluded from this threat. As for what follows this verse, it is His saying: ﴿We have certainly brought you the truth, but most of you are averse to the truth.﴾ The "truth" here means either Islam or the Qur'an, and a Muslim man does not dislike Islam or the Qur'an. Thus it is established that what precedes this verse and what follows it indicates that the intended meaning of "criminals" is the disbelievers. And Allah knows best.

The second issue: He the Exalted described the punishment of Hell, regarding the criminals, with three attributes.

The first: "abiding" (khulud). We have mentioned in many places that it is an expression for a long duration of stay, and it does not necessarily indicate perpetuity.

The second: His saying ﴿It will not be lightened for them﴾, meaning it will not be reduced or diminished. It comes from their saying: "The fever abated from him" (faturat ʿanhu al-humma) when it subsided and its heat decreased.

The third: His saying ﴿and they will be in it in despair﴾. The mubli s (one in despair) is the one who is silent with the silence of one who has despaired of relief. From al-Dahhak: the criminal will be placed in a coffin of fire, then it will be closed upon him, and he will remain in it, abiding, unseen. The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari, the Kashshaf) said: it has been read as (wa-hum fīhā), meaning: and they are in the Fire.

The third issue: al-Qadi argued with His saying: ﴿We did not wrong them, but they were the wrongdoers.﴾ He said: If He created disbelief in them in order to make them enter the Fire, then what is it that He negated by His saying "We did not wrong them"? And what is it that He attributed to them of what He negated from Himself? Would not affirming it as injustice to them be no more than what the people say? If they say: that act did not occur by the power of Allah the Mighty and Majestic alone, but occurred by the power of Allah together with the power of the servant jointly, then it was not an injustice from Allah.

We say: According to you, the power to do injustice necessitates injustice, and the Creator of that power is Allah the Exalted. So it is as if He, the Exalted, when He created in them the power to disbelieve along with creating disbelief, went out of being unjust to them, and that is impossible, because whoever is unjust in an act, when he does with it what necessitates that act, is more deserving of that description. So it is said to al-Qadi: Is the power of the servant suitable for both alternatives, or is it determined for one of the two alternatives? If it is suitable for both alternatives, then if the preference occurs without a preferring cause, the existence of the Creator is necessitated to be denied; and if it requires a preferring cause, the first division returns regarding it, and it must end in a preferring motive which Allah creates in the servant. And if it is determined for one of the two alternatives, then at that point what you have raised against us is binding upon you.

[Page 195]

Know that the man is not one who sees the line of argument and mentions it; rather, the man is one who looks at what precedes the statement and what follows it. If he sees it as coming upon his own school of thought exactly, he does not mention it. And Allah knows best.

The fourth issue: Ibn Masʿud read (yā Mālu) by dropping the kāf for the sake of apocope (tarkhīm). It was said to Ibn ʿAbbas: Ibn Masʿud read: "And they will call, O Mālu." He said: How preoccupied the people of the Fire are from this apocope! It was answered that this apocope was only fitting because it indicates that they had reached such weakness and emaciation that they could not utter from the word except part of it.

The fifth issue: They differed about the manner in which they made their request in His saying: ﴿O Malik, let your Lord put an end to us.﴾ Some of them said: it is by way of wishing. Others said: it is by way of seeking help, since they know that there is no escape for them from that punishment. It was also said: it is not far-fetched to say that because of the severity of what they are in of punishment, they forgot that request and so mentioned it by way of asking. Then He the Exalted explained that Malik says to them: ﴿Indeed, you will remain.﴾ The Qur'an does not say when he answered them: did he answer them immediately, or after a long period? And if it was after that, did that answer come a short time after that request, or a long time? There is nothing to prevent that the answer be delayed, as a way of belittling them and increasing their distress. It is reported from ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿUmar that it was after forty years, from others after a hundred years, and from Ibn ʿAbbas after a thousand years. And Allah knows best the exact measure of that.

Then He the Exalted explained that when Malik answered them with His saying ﴿Indeed, you will remain,﴾ He mentioned after it what is like the reason for that answer, saying: ﴿We have certainly brought you the truth, but most of you are averse to the truth.﴾ What is meant is their aversion toward Muhammad and the Qur'an, and the intensity of their hatred for accepting the true religion. If it is said: How does He say ﴿and they will call, O Malik﴾ after describing them with despair? We say: those are long periods and extended ages, so their conditions vary, and they fall silent at times due to the overwhelming of despair upon them, and they cry for help at times because of the severity of what they suffer. It is narrated that hunger will be inflicted upon the people of the Fire until it balances the punishment they are in, so they say: Call upon Malik, and they call: ﴿And they will call, O Malik, let your Lord put an end to us.﴾

When Allah the Exalted mentioned the manner of their punishment in the Hereafter, He then mentioned the manner of their deceit and the corruption of their inner state in this world, saying: ﴿Or have they decided on a matter? Then indeed, We decide.﴾ The meaning: "Or have they decided" — that is, the polytheists of Mecca have decided upon a matter of their plotting and scheming against the Messenger of Allah — "then indeed, We decide Our plan, just as they decided their plan." Like His saying: ﴿Or do they intend a plot? But those who disbelieved, they are the ones plotted against.﴾ [at-Tur: 42]. Muqatil said: it was revealed concerning their planning to scheme against him in the Dar al-Nadwa (the assembly house of Quraysh), and that is what Allah mentioned in His saying: ﴿And when those who disbelieved plotted against you﴾ [al-Anfal: 30]. We have mentioned the story.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿Or do they think that We do not hear their secret and their private conversation?﴾ The secret (sirr) is what a man speaks to himself or to another in a private place, and the private conversation (najwa) is what they speak among themselves. ﴿Yes,﴾ We hear it and are aware of it. ﴿And Our messengers﴾ — he means the guardian angels — ﴿are recording﴾ those states against them. It is reported from Yahya ibn Muʿadh: Whoever conceals his sins from people, and displays them to One from whom nothing in the heavens is hidden, has made Him the least of those who look at him, and this is one of the signs of hypocrisy.

[Page 196]

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Say: If the Most Merciful had a son, I would be the first of the worshippers.﴾ ﴿Glory be to the Lord of the heavens and the earth, the Lord of the Throne, above what they describe.﴾ ﴿So leave them to wade in falsehood and play, until they meet their Day which they are promised.﴾ ﴿And He is the one in the heaven a God and in the earth a God, and He is the All-Wise, the All-Knowing.﴾ ﴿Blessed is He to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and what is between them, and with Him is the knowledge of the Hour, and to Him you will be returned.﴾ ﴿And those they invoke besides Him have no power of intercession, except one who testifies to the truth while knowing.﴾ ﴿And if you asked them who created them, they would surely say, "Allah." So how are they turned away?﴾ ﴿And [He knows] his saying, "My Lord, these are a people who do not believe."﴾ ﴿So turn away from them and say, "Peace." But they will soon know.﴾ And in it are issues:

The first issue: Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read (وُلْدٌ) with a ḍammah on the wāw and sukūn on the lām, while the rest read it with a fatḥah on the wāw. In ﴿fa-anā awwalu l-ʿābidīn﴾, Nāfiʿ read (فَأنا) with a long fatḥah on the nūn, while the rest read it without lengthening.

The second issue: Know that people thought that His saying ﴿Say: If the Most Merciful had a son, I would be the first of the worshippers﴾, if we take it according to its apparent meaning, then it entails the occurrence of doubt regarding the affirmation of a son for Allah the Exalted, and that is impossible. Therefore they were obliged to seek an interpretation of the verse. But in my view the matter is not so, and there is nothing in the apparent wording that requires departing from the apparent meaning. Its explanation is that His saying ﴿If the Most Merciful had a son, I would be the first of the worshippers﴾ is a conditional proposition (qaḍiyyah sharṭiyyah). A conditional proposition is composed of two declarative propositions, a particle of condition (ḥarf al-sharṭ) being placed before one of them and a particle of consequence (ḥarf al-jazāʾ) before the other; thus by their combination a single proposition results. An example of this is this verse, for His saying ﴿If the Most Merciful had a son, I would be the first of the worshippers﴾ is a proposition composed of two propositions: one of them is His saying ﴿If the Most Merciful had a son﴾, and the second is His saying ﴿I would be the first of the worshippers﴾. Then He placed the particle of condition, which is the word (إنْ), before the first proposition, and the particle of consequence, which is the fāʾ, before the second; thus from their combination there resulted a single proposition, which is the conditional proposition.

Having understood this, we say: a conditional proposition does not convey anything except that the condition necessitates the consequence. It does not imply that the condition is true or false, nor that the consequence is true or false. Rather, we say: a true conditional proposition may be composed of two true propositions, or of two false propositions, or of a false condition and a true consequence, or of a true condition and a false consequence. As for the fourth case, namely that a true conditional proposition is composed of a true condition and a false consequence, this is impossible.

Let us illustrate examples of these four categories. When we say: "If man is an animal, then man is a body," this is a true conditional, and it is composed of two true propositions: one of them is our statement "Man is an animal," and the second is our statement "Man is a body." When we say: "If five is even, then it is divisible into two equal parts," this is a true conditional, but it is composed of our statement "Five is even" and our statement "Five is divisible into two equal parts," and both are false. That both are false does not prevent the entailment of one by the other from being true, and we have said that a conditional proposition conveys nothing but mere entailment. When we say: "If man is a stone, then he is a body," this is also true, but it is composed of a false condition, which is our statement "Man is a stone," and a true part, which is our statement "Man is a body."

[Page 197]

This is permissible because falsehood may be such that, if it is supposed to occur, a truth follows from it. If we suppose that man is a stone, it necessarily follows that he is a body; so this is a false condition entailing a true consequence.

As for the fourth category, namely the composition of a true conditional from a true condition and a false consequence, this is impossible, because this composition would entail that the truth necessitates falsehood, and that is impossible. This differs from the third category, for there it entails that falsehood necessitates truth, and that is not impossible.

Having understood this principle, let us return to the verse and say: His saying ﴿If the Most Merciful had a son, I would be the first of the worshippers﴾ is a true conditional proposition composed of a false condition and a false consequence, because our statement "The Most Merciful had a son" is false, and our statement "I am the first of the worshippers" for that son is also false. Yet we have shown that both being false does not prevent the entailment of one by the other from being true, as we exemplified in our statement: "If five is even, then it is divisible into two equal parts." Thus it is established that this statement has no impediment to being taken according to its apparent meaning, and its meaning is: If the Most Merciful had a son, I would be the first of the worshippers of that son, for when a king has a son, just as his servant must serve him, so too the king must serve his son. And we have shown that this composition does not indicate acknowledgment of whether a son is affirmed or not.

Something closely related to this category is His saying ﴿Had there been in them [the heavens and the earth] gods other than Allah, they would both have been ruined﴾ [al-Anbiyāʾ: 22]. This statement is a conditional proposition, its condition being our statement "there are in them gods," and its consequence being our statement "they would both have been ruined." The condition in itself is false, and the consequence is also false, because the truth is that there are no gods in them. The word (لَوْ) conveys the negation of one thing due to the negation of another, since they were not ruined. Yet even though the condition is false and the consequence is false, the entailment of that consequence by that condition is true. So too here.

If they say: The difference is that here He stated this conditional with the form (لَوْ), saying ﴿Had there been gods in them﴾, and the word (لَوْ) conveys the negation of one thing due to the negation of another; whereas in the verse we are interpreting, He stated the word (إنْ), and this word does not convey the negation of one thing due to the negation of another, but rather conveys doubt as to whether the condition has occurred or not. And the occurrence of such doubt for the Messenger is not possible.

We say: The difference you mention is correct, but our purpose is to show that it does not follow from the conditional being true that its two parts are both true or both false, as we have established. As for your statement that the word (إنْ) conveys whether the condition has occurred or not, we say: this is disputed, for the particle (إنْ) is the particle of condition, and the particle of condition conveys nothing except that the condition entails the consequence. As for showing whether that condition is known to occur or doubtful in its occurrence, the wording has no indication of this at all.

Thus it becomes clear from the discussions we have summarized that this statement can be taken according to its apparent meaning in every respect, and that there is no need at all for interpretation. The meaning is that He, the Exalted, said: "Say, O Muḥammad (ﷺ), ﴿If the Most Merciful had a son, I would be the first of the worshippers﴾ of that son, and I would be the first to serve him." The purpose of this statement is to show that I do not deny His son out of obstinacy and contention. For if proof were to be established for the existence of this son, I would acknowledge him and admit the obligation of serving him. But this son has not been found, and no proof for his existence has been established at all; so how can I affirm him? Rather, a decisive proof stands for his non-existence; so how can I affirm him, and how can I acknowledge his existence? This statement is clear and complete, needing no interpretation or departure from the apparent meaning at all. This is what I hold on this point.

It is related from al-Suddī among the exegetes that he used to say: taking this verse according to its apparent meaning is possible, and there is no need for interpretation. The explanation we have given indicates that what he said is the truth. As for those who hold that interpretation is necessary, they have mentioned several opinions:

The first: al-Wāḥidī said: The interpretations of this verse are many, and the strongest is to say that the meaning is: "If the Most Merciful had a son, according to your claim, then I am the first of the worshippers," that is, the first of those who affirm Allah's oneness and deny your attribution of a son to Him.

[Page 198]

Someone may say: Either the sentence means, "If it is established in reality that the Most Merciful has a son, then I am the first to deny it," or it means, "If you claim that the Most Merciful has a son, then I am the first to deny it." The first is false, because the existence of a thing in itself does not entail that the Messenger denies it; for his saying "If a thing is established in itself, then I am the first to deny it" entails his persistence in lying and ignorance, and that does not befit the Messenger. The second is also false, because whether they affirm a son for Allah or not, the Messenger denies that son. Thus their claim had no effect on the Messenger's denial of that son, and it was not appropriate to make their affirmation of a son the cause of the Messenger's denial of the son.

The second opinion: They said: its meaning is ﴿If the Most Merciful had a son, I would be the first of the worshippers﴾, the (ʿābidīn) here meaning the "disdainful" (ʾānifīn), those who are disdainful of having a son. From (ʿabida), one who is "ʿabid" and "ʿābid" is one whose disdain becomes intense. Some reciters read (عَبِدِينَ).

Know that the question stated above remains here. For if the meaning is: "If the Most Merciful had a son in reality, then I would be the first to be disdainful of acknowledging him," this entails persistence in ignorance and lying. And if the meaning is: "If the Most Merciful had a son according to your claim and belief, then I would be the first to be disdainful," this conditional is invalid, because this disdain exists whether that claim and belief occur or not. And since the matter is so, this conditional is not permissible.

The third opinion: Some said: the word (إنْ) here is the negative particle, and the meaning is: "The Most Merciful had no son; I am the first of the monotheists among the people of Makkah in affirming that He has no son."

Know that resorting to these remote interpretations is only out of necessity, and we have shown that there is absolutely no necessity; therefore it was not permissible to turn to them. And Allah knows best.

Then the Exalted said: ﴿Glory be to the Lord of the heavens and the earth, the Lord of the Throne, above what they describe.﴾ The meaning is that the God of the universe must necessarily exist by His own essence, and whatever is so is a single absolute unity that admits of no division in any way. A son is the separation from a thing of a part of its parts, such that from that part there comes into being a person like it. This is conceivable only of things whose essence admits of division and partition. Since this is impossible with respect to the God of the universe, the affirmation of a son for Him is impossible. When He mentioned this decisive proof, He said: ﴿So leave them to wade in falsehood and play, until they meet their Day which they are promised.﴾ The purpose of this is a threat. The meaning is: I have already mentioned the decisive argument against what they claim, but they have not paid attention to it, because they are absorbed in seeking wealth, status and leadership. So leave them in that falsehood and play, until they reach that Day in which they were promised what they were promised. The purpose of this is a threat.

* * *

Then the Exalted said: ﴿And He is the one in the heaven a God and in the earth a God﴾, and in it there are discussions:

The first discussion: Abū ʿAlī said: I examined what the word (إلَهٌ) is made nominative by, and I found that its nominative case is valid if it is the predicate of an omitted subject (mubtadaʾ). The estimated sentence is: "And He is the one who is in the heaven, He is a God."

The second discussion: This verse is among the strongest proofs that He, the Exalted, is not settled in the heaven. For the Exalted showed by this verse that His being God of the heaven is like His being God of the earth. Since He is God of the earth while not being settled in it, so likewise He must be God of the heaven while not being settled in it. [Page 196]

So how are they turned away?﴾ ﴿And [He knows] his saying, "My Lord, these are a people who do not believe."﴾ ﴿So turn away from them and say, "Peace." But they will soon know.﴾ And in it are issues:

The first issue: Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read (وُلْدٌ) with a ḍammah on the wāw and sukūn on the lām, while the rest read it with a fatḥah on the wāw. In ﴿fa-anā awwalu l-ʿābidīn﴾, Nāfiʿ read (فَأنا) with a long fatḥah on the nūn, while the rest read it without lengthening.

The second issue: Know that people thought that His saying ﴿Say: If the Most Merciful had a son, I would be the first of the worshippers﴾, if we take it according to its apparent meaning, then it entails the occurrence of doubt regarding the affirmation of a son for Allah the Exalted, and that is impossible. Therefore they were obliged to seek an interpretation of the verse. But in my view the matter is not so, and there is nothing in the apparent wording that requires departing from the apparent meaning. Its explanation is that His saying ﴿If the Most Merciful had a son, I would be the first of the worshippers﴾ is a conditional proposition (qaḍiyyah sharṭiyyah). A conditional proposition is composed of two declarative propositions, a particle of condition (ḥarf al-sharṭ) being placed before one of them and a particle of consequence (ḥarf al-jazāʾ) before the other; thus by their combination a single proposition results. An example of this is this verse, for His saying ﴿If the Most Merciful had a son, I would be the first of the worshippers﴾ is a proposition composed of two propositions: one of them is His saying ﴿If the Most Merciful had a son﴾, and the second is His saying ﴿I would be the first of the worshippers﴾. Then He placed the particle of condition, which is the word (إنْ), before the first proposition, and the particle of consequence, which is the fāʾ, before the second; thus from their combination there resulted a single proposition, which is the conditional proposition.

Having understood this, we say: a conditional proposition does not convey anything except that the condition necessitates the consequence. It does not imply that the condition is true or false, nor that the consequence is true or false. Rather, we say: a true conditional proposition may be composed of two true propositions, or of two false propositions, or of a false condition and a true consequence, or of a true condition and a false consequence. As for the fourth case, namely that a true conditional proposition is composed of a true condition and a false consequence, this is impossible.

Let us illustrate examples of these four categories. When we say: "If man is an animal, then man is a body," this is a true conditional, and it is composed of two true propositions: one of them is our statement "Man is an animal," and the second is our statement "Man is a body." When we say: "If five is even, then it is divisible into two equal parts," this is a true conditional, but it is composed of our statement "Five is even" and our statement "Five is divisible into two equal parts," and both are false. That both are false does not prevent the entailment of one by the other from being true, and we have said that a conditional proposition conveys nothing but mere entailment. When we say: "If man is a stone, then he is a body," this is also true, but it is composed of a false condition, which is our statement "Man is a stone," and a true part, which is our statement "Man is a body."

[Page 197]

This is permissible because falsehood may be such that, if it is supposed to occur, a truth follows from it. If we suppose that man is a stone, it necessarily follows that he is a body; so this is a false condition entailing a true consequence.

As for the fourth category, namely the composition of a true conditional from a true condition and a false consequence, this is impossible, because this composition would entail that the truth necessitates falsehood, and that is impossible. This differs from the third category, for there it entails that falsehood necessitates truth, and that is not impossible.

Having understood this principle, let us return to the verse and say: His saying ﴿If the Most Merciful had a son, I would be the first of the worshippers﴾ is a true conditional proposition composed of a false condition and a false consequence, because our statement "The Most Merciful had a son" is false, and our statement "I am the first of the worshippers" for that son is also false. Yet we have shown that both being false does not prevent the entailment of one by the other from being true, as we exemplified in our statement: "If five is even, then it is divisible into two equal parts." Thus it is established that this statement has no impediment to being taken according to its apparent meaning, and its meaning is: If the Most Merciful had a son, I would be the first of the worshippers of that son, for when a king has a son, just as his servant must serve him, so too the king must serve his son. And we have shown that this composition does not indicate acknowledgment of whether a son is affirmed or not.

Something closely related to this category is His saying ﴿Had there been in them [the heavens and the earth] gods other than Allah, they would both have been ruined﴾ [al-Anbiyāʾ: 22]. This statement is a conditional proposition, its condition being our statement "there are in them gods," and its consequence being our statement "they would both have been ruined." The condition in itself is false, and the consequence is also false, because the truth is that there are no gods in them. The word (لَوْ) conveys the negation of one thing due to the negation of another, since they were not ruined. Yet even though the condition is false and the consequence is false, the entailment of that consequence by that condition is true. So too here.

If they say: The difference is that here He stated this conditional with the form (لَوْ), saying ﴿Had there been gods in them﴾, and the word (لَوْ) conveys the negation of one thing due to the negation of another; whereas in the verse we are interpreting, He stated the word (إنْ), and this word does not convey the negation of one thing due to the negation of another, but rather conveys doubt as to whether the condition has occurred or not. And the occurrence of such doubt for the Messenger is not possible.

We say: The difference you mention is correct, but our purpose is to show that it does not follow from the conditional being true that its two parts are both true or both false, as we have established. As for your statement that the word (إنْ) conveys whether the condition has occurred or not, we say: this is disputed, for the particle (إنْ) is the particle of condition, and the particle of condition conveys nothing except that the condition entails the consequence. As for showing whether that condition is known to occur or doubtful in its occurrence, the wording has no indication of this at all.

Thus it becomes clear from the discussions we have summarized that this statement can be taken according to its apparent meaning in every respect, and that there is no need at all for interpretation. The meaning is that He, the Exalted, said: "Say, O Muḥammad (ﷺ), ﴿If the Most Merciful had a son, I would be the first of the worshippers﴾ of that son, and I would be the first to serve him." The purpose of this statement is to show that I do not deny His son out of obstinacy and contention. For if proof were to be established for the existence of this son, I would acknowledge him and admit the obligation of serving him. But this son has not been found, and no proof for his existence has been established at all; so how can I affirm him? Rather, a decisive proof stands for his non-existence; so how can I affirm him, and how can I acknowledge his existence? This statement is clear and complete, needing no interpretation or departure from the apparent meaning at all. This is what I hold on this point.

It is related from al-Suddī among the exegetes that he used to say: taking this verse according to its apparent meaning is possible, and there is no need for interpretation. The explanation we have given indicates that what he said is the truth. As for those who hold that interpretation is necessary, they have mentioned several opinions:

The first: al-Wāḥidī said: The interpretations of this verse are many, and the strongest is to say that the meaning is: "If the Most Merciful had a son, according to your claim, then I am the first of the worshippers," that is, the first of those who affirm Allah's oneness and deny your attribution of a son to Him.

[Page 198]

Someone may say: Either the sentence means, "If it is established in reality that the Most Merciful has a son, then I am the first to deny it," or it means, "If you claim that the Most Merciful has a son, then I am the first to deny it." The first is false, because the existence of a thing in itself does not entail that the Messenger denies it; for his saying "If a thing is established in itself, then I am the first to deny it" entails his persistence in lying and ignorance, and that does not befit the Messenger. The second is also false, because whether they affirm a son for Allah or not, the Messenger denies that son. Thus their claim had no effect on the Messenger's denial of that son, and it was not appropriate to make their affirmation of a son the cause of the Messenger's denial of the son.

The second opinion: They said: its meaning is ﴿If the Most Merciful had a son, I would be the first of the worshippers﴾, the (ʿābidīn) here meaning the "disdainful" (ʾānifīn), those who are disdainful of having a son. From (ʿabida), one who is "ʿabid" and "ʿābid" is one whose disdain becomes intense. Some reciters read (عَبِدِينَ).

Know that the question stated above remains here. For if the meaning is: "If the Most Merciful had a son in reality, then I would be the first to be disdainful of acknowledging him," this entails persistence in ignorance and lying. And if the meaning is: "If the Most Merciful had a son according to your claim and belief, then I would be the first to be disdainful," this conditional is invalid, because this disdain exists whether that claim and belief occur or not. And since the matter is so, this conditional is not permissible.

The third opinion: Some said: the word (إنْ) here is the negative particle, and the meaning is: "The Most Merciful had no son; I am the first of the monotheists among the people of Makkah in affirming that He has no son."

Know that resorting to these remote interpretations is only out of necessity, and we have shown that there is absolutely no necessity; therefore it was not permissible to turn to them. And Allah knows best.

Then the Exalted said: ﴿Glory be to the Lord of the heavens and the earth, the Lord of the Throne, above what they describe.﴾ The meaning is that the God of the universe must necessarily exist by His own essence, and whatever is so is a single absolute unity that admits of no division in any way. When He mentioned this decisive proof, He said: ﴿So leave them to wade in falsehood and play, until they meet their Day which they are promised.﴾ The purpose of this is a threat. The meaning is: I have already mentioned the decisive argument against what they claim, but they have not paid attention to it, because they are absorbed in seeking wealth, status and leadership. So leave them in that falsehood and play, until they reach that Day in which they were promised what they were promised. The purpose of this is a threat.

An example of this is this verse, for His saying ﴿If the Most Merciful had a son, I would be the first of the worshippers﴾ is a proposition composed of two propositions: one of them is His saying ﴿If the Most Merciful had a son﴾, and the second is His saying ﴿I would be the first of the worshippers﴾. Then He placed the particle of condition, which is the word (إنْ), before the first proposition, and the particle of consequence, which is the fāʾ, before the second; thus from their combination there resulted a single proposition, which is the conditional proposition.

Having understood this, we say: a conditional proposition does not convey anything except that the condition necessitates the consequence. It does not imply that the condition is true or false, nor that the consequence is true or false. Rather, we say: a true conditional proposition may be composed of two true propositions, or of two false propositions, or of a false condition and a true consequence, or of a true condition and a false consequence. As for the fourth case, namely that a true conditional proposition is composed of a true condition and a false consequence, this is impossible.

Let us illustrate examples of these four categories. When we say: "If man is an animal, then man is a body," this is a true conditional, and it is composed of two true propositions: one of them is our statement "Man is an animal," and the second is our statement "Man is a body." When we say: "If five is even, then it is divisible into two equal parts," this is a true conditional, but it is composed of our statement "Five is even" and our statement "Five is divisible into two equal parts," and both are false. That both are false does not prevent the entailment of one by the other from being true, and we have said that a conditional proposition conveys nothing but mere entailment. When we say: "If man is a stone, then he is a body," this is also true, but it is composed of a false condition, which is our statement "Man is a stone," and a true part, which is our statement "Man is a body."

[Page 197]

The condition in itself is false, and the consequence is also false, because the truth is that there are no gods in them. Thus it becomes clear from the discussions we have summarized that this statement can be taken according to its apparent meaning in every respect, and that there is no need at all for interpretation. The meaning is that He, the Exalted, said: "Say, O Muḥammad (ﷺ), ﴿If the Most Merciful had a son, I would be the first of the worshippers﴾ of that son, and I would be the first to serve him." The purpose of this statement is to show that I do not deny His son out of obstinacy and contention. But this son has not been found, and no proof for his existence has been established at all; so how can I affirm him? Rather, a decisive proof stands for his non-existence; so how can I affirm him, and how can I acknowledge his existence? This statement is clear and complete, needing no interpretation or departure from the apparent meaning at all. This is what I hold on this point.

The first: al-Wāḥidī said: The interpretations of this verse are many, and the strongest is to say that the meaning is: "If the Most Merciful had a son, according to your claim, then I am the first of the worshippers," that is, the first of those who affirm Allah's oneness and deny your attribution of a son to Him.

[Page 198]

Someone may say: Either the sentence means, "If it is established in reality that the Most Merciful has a son, then I am the first to deny it," or it means, "If you claim that the Most Merciful has a son, then I am the first to deny it." Someone may say: Either the sentence means, "If it is established in reality that the Most Merciful has a son, then I am the first to deny it," or it means, "If you claim that the Most Merciful has a son, then I am the first to deny it." The first is false, because the existence of a thing in itself does not entail that the Messenger denies it; for his saying "If a thing is established in itself, then I am the first to deny it" entails his persistence in lying and ignorance, and that does not befit the Messenger. The second is also false, because whether they affirm a son for Allah or not, the Messenger denies that son. Thus their claim had no effect on the Messenger's denial of that son, and it was not appropriate to make their affirmation of a son the cause of the Messenger's denial of the son.

The second opinion: They said: its meaning is ﴿If the Most Merciful had a son, I would be the first of the worshippers﴾, the (ʿābidīn) here meaning the "disdainful" (ʾānifīn), those who are disdainful of having a son. From (ʿabida), one who is "ʿabid" and "ʿābid" is one whose disdain becomes intense. Some reciters read (عَبِدِينَ).

Know that the question stated above remains here. For if the meaning is: "If the Most Merciful had a son in reality, then I would be the first to be disdainful of acknowledging him," this entails persistence in ignorance and lying. And if the meaning is: "If the Most Merciful had a son according to your claim and belief, then I would be the first to be disdainful," this conditional is invalid, because this disdain exists whether that claim and belief occur or not. And since the matter is so, this conditional is not permissible.

The third opinion: Some said: the word (إنْ) here is the negative particle, and the meaning is: "The Most Merciful had no son; I am the first of the monotheists among the people of Makkah in affirming that He has no son."

Know that resorting to these remote interpretations is only out of necessity, and we have shown that there is absolutely no necessity; therefore it was not permissible to turn to them. And Allah knows best.

Then the Exalted said: ﴿Glory be to the Lord of the heavens and the earth, the Lord of the Throne, above what they describe.﴾ The meaning is that the God of the universe must necessarily exist by His own essence, and whatever is so is a single absolute unity that admits of no division in any way. A son is the separation from a thing of a part of its parts, such that from that part there comes into being a person like it. This is conceivable only of things whose essence admits of division and partition. Since this is impossible with respect to the God of the universe, the affirmation of a son for Him is impossible. When He mentioned this decisive proof, He said: ﴿So leave them to wade in falsehood and play, until they meet their Day which they are promised.﴾ The purpose of this is a threat. The meaning is: I have already mentioned the decisive argument against what they claim, but they have not paid attention to it, because they are absorbed in seeking wealth, status and leadership. So leave them in that falsehood and play, until they reach that Day in which they were promised what they were promised. The purpose of this is a threat.

* * *

Then the Exalted said: ﴿And He is the one in the heaven a God and in the earth a God﴾, and in it there are discussions:

The first discussion: Abū ʿAlī said: I examined what the word (إلَهٌ) is made nominative by, and I found that its nominative case is valid if it is the predicate of an omitted subject (mubtadaʾ). The estimated sentence is: "And He is the one who is in the heaven, He is a God."

The second discussion: This verse is among the strongest proofs that He, the Exalted, is not settled in the heaven. For the Exalted showed by this verse that His being God of the heaven is like His being God of the earth. Since He is God of the earth while not being settled in it, so likewise He must be God of the heaven while not being settled in it. If it is said: What connection does this statement have with the negation of a son from Allah?

[Page 199]

Its connection to this is that God, exalted is He, created Jesus by the mere command "Be," and he was, without the intermediary of a drop of semen or a father. It is as if it were said: this degree alone does not necessitate that Jesus be a son of God, glory be to Him, because this meaning is present in the creation of the heavens and the earth and what is between them, while sonship is absent there.
* * *
Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And He is the All-Wise, the All-Knowing﴾. We have mentioned in Surat al-An'am that His being All-Wise and All-Knowing contradicts the existence of a child for Him.

Then He said: ﴿Blessed is He to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and what is between them, and with whom is the knowledge of the Hour, and to whom you will be returned.﴾ Know that His saying "tabaraka" (blessed) is either derived from permanence and endurance (al-thabat wa'l-baqa'), or derived from abundance of good (kathrat al-khayr). Under either of the two interpretations, each of these two meanings contradicts the sonship of Jesus, peace be upon him, to God Most High. For if what is meant is permanence and endurance, then Jesus, peace be upon him, was not necessarily everlasting and enduring, since he came into being after not having existed. Moreover, according to the Christians, he was killed and died, and whoever is like that has no kinship or resemblance with the Eternal, Everlasting One, so it is impossible that he be His son. And if what is meant by blessing is abundance of good, such as being the creator of the heavens and the earth and what is between them, then Jesus was not like that; rather he needed food. And according to the Christians, he was afraid of the Jews, and eventually they seized him and killed him. So how could one whose description is this be a son of Him who created the heavens and the earth and what is between them?!

* * *
As for His saying: ﴿And with Him is the knowledge of the Hour﴾, its purpose is that, having explained the perfection of His power, He likewise explained the perfection of His knowledge. The aim is to alert that whoever is perfect in essence, knowledge and power to the degree we have described cannot have a son who is in weakness and lacks awareness of the conditions of the world to the degree the Christians ascribe.

When God Most High had elaborated on the denial of offspring, He followed it with the explanation of the denial of partners, saying: ﴿And those they invoke besides Him have no power of intercession, except he who testifies to the truth while they know﴾. The exegetes have mentioned two opinions regarding this verse:

The first: that those invoked besides Him are the angels, Jesus and Uzair, and the meaning is that the angels, Jesus and Uzair do not intercede except for one who testifies to the truth. It is narrated that al-Nadr ibn al-Harith and a group with him said: "If what Muhammad says is true, then we will take the angels as patrons, for they are more worthy of intercession than Muhammad." So God revealed this verse, saying: These cannot intercede for anyone. Then He made an exception, saying: ﴿except he who testifies to the truth﴾. The meaning according to this view is that these do not intercede except for one who testifies to the truth; the preposition "li" (for) is then understood. Or it may be said that the implied phrase is: except the intercession of one who testifies to the truth, so the noun is omitted. This is according to the dialect of those who construct "shafa'a" without "li", saying "shafa'tu fulanan" meaning "shafa'tu lahu" (I interceded for him), just as one says "kallamtuhu" and "kallamtu lahu", and "nasahtuhu" and "nasahtu lahu".

The second opinion: that those invoked besides Him are every object of worship besides God, and His saying ﴿except he who testifies to the truth﴾ refers to the angels, Jesus and Uzair. The meaning is that the things the unbelievers worshipped have no power of intercession except for those who testified to the truth, namely the angels, Jesus and Uzair, for they have intercession with God and a station. And the meaning of "he who testifies to the truth" is: he who testifies that there is no god but God.

* * *
Then God Most High said: ﴿while they know﴾. This restriction indicates that testimony by the tongue alone is of no benefit whatsoever. Those who hold that the faith of one who merely follows authority (al-muqallid) is of no benefit at all have argued from this verse, saying: God has made clear that testimony is not beneficial unless knowledge accompanies it, and knowledge is the certainty such that if its possessor were cast into doubt about it, he would not be doubtful; and this is not attained except through proof. Therefore it is established that the faith of one who follows authority is of no benefit whatsoever.

Page 200
Then God Most High said: ﴿And if you asked them who created them, they would surely say: God. Then how are they turned away?﴾ Concerning this there are two issues:

The first issue: Some people thought that this verse and similar ones in the Qur'an indicate that the people are compelled to acknowledge the existence of a God for the world. Al-Jubba'i said: This is not correct, for the people of Pharaoh said: "He has no god other than Himself," and the people of Abraham said: ﴿And indeed we are in doubt about that to which you invite us﴾ [Ibrahim: 9]. It is said to them: We do not concede that the people of Pharaoh were deniers of the existence of God. The proof of our view is His saying: ﴿And they denied them, though their souls were convinced of them, out of injustice﴾ [al-Naml: 14], and Moses said to Pharaoh: ﴿You have certainly known that none has sent these down except the Lord of the heavens and the earth as evidence﴾ [al-Isra': 102]. The reading with a fatha on the ta' in "'alimta" indicates that Pharaoh was knowing of God. As for the people of Abraham, when they said: ﴿And indeed we are in doubt about that to which you invite us﴾, it refers to doubt about the resurrection, the obligations and prophethood.

The third issue: Know that He mentioned this statement at the beginning of this surah and at its end. The purpose is to alert that they believed the Creator of the world and the Creator of the animals is God Most High; so how did they, with this belief, proceed to worship base bodies and wicked idols that neither harm nor benefit, but are pure inanimate matter?!

* * *
As for His saying: ﴿Then how are they turned away?﴾, its meaning is: why do you lie against God, saying that God commanded us to worship idols? Some of our companions have used this to argue that their falsehood is not from them but from others, by His saying: ﴿Then how are they turned away?﴾. Al-Qadi answered that whoever goes astray in understanding speech or in the road is asked: "Where is he taking you?" meaning: "Where are you going?" The companions answered that the saying of the speaker "Where is he taking you?" apparently indicates that another person has taken him away, so diverting the speech from its literal meaning contradicts the apparent original sense. Furthermore, the one who took him away is the one who created that motive in his heart, and it has been established by clear proof that the creator of that motive is God Most High.

* * *
Then God Most High said: ﴿And His saying: "My Lord, these are a people who do not believe"﴾. Concerning this there are several discussions:

The first: Most readers read "wa-qīlahu" with a fatha on the lam, while 'Asim and Hamza read it with a kasra on the lam. Al-Wahidi said: Some readers outside the seven read it with a raf' (nominative). As for those who read it in the accusative, al-Akhfash and al-Farra' mentioned two views concerning it: One: that it is accusative as a verbal noun, with the implied sense: "and he said his saying and complained his complaint to his Lord," meaning the Prophet ﷺ, so "qīlahu" is governed by an implied "qāla". The second: that it is conjoined to what precedes it in His saying: "We do not hear their secret and their private talk... and his saying". Al-Zajjaj mentioned a third view, saying: it is accusative in the position of "al-sa'a" (the Hour), because His saying ﴿and with Him is the knowledge of the Hour﴾ means that He knows the Hour, and the sense is: He knows the Hour and His saying, like your saying: "I wondered at the striking of Zayd and 'Amr." As for the reading with a genitive, al-Akhfash, al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: it is conjoined to "al-sa'a" (the Hour), that is: with Him is the knowledge of the Hour, and the knowledge of His saying: "O Lord." Al-Mubarrad said: conjunction with an accusative is good even if the conjoined word is far from the word it is conjoined to, because it is permissible to separate the accusative from its governing word, and the genitive permits this too, though with ugliness. As for the reading with a nominative, there are two views:

The first: that "wa-qīlihi" is the subject (mubtada') and its predicate is what follows.

The second: that it is conjoined to "'ilm al-sa'a" (the knowledge of the Hour), with the omission of an annexed noun, the meaning being: "And with Him is the knowledge of the Hour and the knowledge of His saying." The author of the "Kashshaf" said: These views are not strong in meaning, especially given the intervening of a parenthetical clause between the conjoined and the conjoined-to. He then mentioned another view and claimed it stronger than what preceded, namely that the accusative and genitive are by the implied and omitted particle of oath, while the nominative is in the manner of their saying "aymunu-llah", "amanatu-llah" and "yamin-Allah", with His saying ﴿Indeed these are a people who do not believe﴾ being the answer to the oath, as if it were said:

Page 201
"And He swore by His saying: 'O Lord,' or 'and His saying: O Lord, is my oath.'" I say: what the author of the "Kashshaf" mentioned is also contrived. Here there is an implied element of which the Qur'an is full, namely the implied "udhkur" (remember), so the sense is: "And remember His saying: 'O Lord.'" As for the reading with a genitive, the sense is: "And remember the time of His saying: 'O Lord.'" And if it is necessary to posit an implied element, then implying something for which the Qur'an's custom is to be implied is more fitting than other things. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that in explaining His saying ﴿And His saying: "My Lord"﴾, he said the meaning is: "And it was said: O Lord," and the "ha'" (his) is superfluous.

The second discussion: "al-qīl" is a verbal noun like "al-qawl", and from it is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "He forbade qīl and qāl (idle talk)." Al-Layth said: The Arabs say: "There is much qīl and qāl in it." Shamir narrated from Abu Zayd: one says "ma ahsana qaylaka wa-qawlaka wa-qālaka wa-qālatika wa-maqālatika," five forms.

The third discussion: The pronoun in "qīlihi" refers to the Messenger of God ﷺ.

The fourth discussion: When the Prophet ﷺ became distressed with them and recognized their persistence, he informed about them that they are a people who do not believe, which is close to what God related about Noah, that he said: ﴿My Lord, indeed they have disobeyed me and followed one whose wealth and children increase him only in loss﴾ [Nuh: 21].

Then God said to him: ﴿So turn away from them﴾, commanding him to pardon them, and implicitly forbidding him from invoking punishment upon them. Al-safh is turning away.

* * *
Then He said: ﴿And say: Peace﴾. Sibawayh said: its meaning is only disengagement (al-mutarakah), and its parallel is Abraham's saying to his father: ﴿Peace be upon you; I will ask forgiveness for you from my Lord﴾ [Maryam: 47], and like His saying: ﴿Peace be upon you; we do not seek the ignorant﴾ [al-Qasas: 55].

His saying: ﴿But they will come to know﴾, its purpose is a threat, and concerning it there are issues:

The first issue: Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read "ta'lamun" with the ta' as address, while the rest read it with the ya' as a reference to a people who do not believe.

The second issue: Some people used this verse to argue that it is permissible to greet an unbeliever with peace. I say: if this inference is sound, then it necessitates limiting oneself to the mere saying "Salam", and that one says to a believer "Salamun 'alaykum"; the purpose is to alert to the greeting which is mentioned for both the Muslim and the unbeliever.

The third issue: Ibn 'Abbas said: His saying, "So turn away from them and say: Peace," is abrogated by the verse of the sword. In my view, positing abrogation in such passages is problematic, because a command yields the act only once; if he performs it once, the force of the wording has been fulfilled, so what need is there to posit abrogation? Also, a similar case is the well-known "immediate oath" (yamin al-fawr) among the jurists, which indicates that a wording may be restricted according to the indication of customary context; and if that is so, there is no need to posit abrogation. And God knows best what is correct.

Our master the author, may the clouds of mercy and good pleasure be upon him, said: The tafsir of this surah was completed on Sunday, the eleventh of Dhu al-Hijjah, in the year six hundred and three, and praise be to God first and last, outwardly and inwardly, and blessings upon His honored angels and the prophets and messengers, especially upon Muhammad ﷺ, his family and all his companions, forever and ever.
